### Presidential Reversal: What the Record Shows About Each Administration Undoing the Last

Filed as: Special Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-14T12:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-14-presidential-reversal-record.html

Special Report

Executive Orders · The Regulatory Freeze · The Congressional Review Act · The Elections of 1980, 2022, and 2024

Objective

Presidential Reversal: What the Record Shows About Each Administration Undoing the Last

Every president who has taken the White House from the other party since 1981 has opened by stopping, withdrawing, or revoking the work of the man before him, using four instruments the record defines: the revocation order, the regulatory freeze memorandum, the Congressional Review Act disapproval, and the withdrawal of pending rules. The counts have climbed across four decades. In their first hundred days, presidents revoked five prior executive orders in 2001, nine in 2009, thirteen in 2017, and sixty-seven in 2021; on January 20, 2025, a single order revoked seventy-eight. The Congressional Review Act, used once in its first twenty years, has now been used twenty-three times in the present Congress. Each administration's documents give its reasons in its own words.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Saturday, November 14, 2026.

Reversal is the standing first act of American government, and it is conducted in paperwork. Since 1981, every president who has taken office from the opposing party has begun his administration by undoing pieces of his predecessor's work, and the undoing runs through four instruments whose texts survive: the executive order that revokes earlier executive orders by number; the regulatory freeze memorandum that stops the pipeline of unfinished rules on the first day; the Congressional Review Act resolution by which Congress and the new president together void a finished rule and bar its return in substantially the same form; and the withdrawal or postponement of rules still pending when the government changes hands. The American Presidency Project's count of the first hundred days shows the volume rising across the modern transitions: five prior executive orders revoked in 2001, nine in 2009, thirteen in 2017, and sixty-seven in 2021, when half of the new president's executive orders carried a revocation inside them. In January 2025 the bulk rescission became a document of its own: Executive Order 14148, signed on the first day, revoked seventy-eight orders and memoranda of the previous administration in a single list, and a second order eight weeks later revoked eighteen more. Congress's instrument has followed the same curve: the Congressional Research Service counts twenty successful disapprovals in the Act's first twenty-eight years—one in 2001, sixteen in 2017–2018, three in 2021—and the trackers of the present Congress count twenty-three more since January 2025. Each era's documents state the era's reasons in the era's vocabulary, and this report prints them from the documents. The elections held in the years of high inflation stand in the same file, and the desk prints those numbers beside the reversal counts, drawing no line between them. The record closes with the forward state of the instruments: reversal is now announced before inaugurations, the current administration continued rescinding through the autumn of 2025, and the statute's own carryover provision has already loaded the next Congress's window with the present administration's late rules.

The four instruments

The first instrument is the revocation clause. An executive order governs until a later president revokes it, and the revocation is ordinarily one sentence inside a successor order: a list of numbers, followed by the words “are hereby revoked.” Because a president's orders bind only the executive branch and rest on his own authority, a successor of either party may strike them at any hour of his tenure, and the Federal Register preserves each strike beside the order it struck. The second instrument works earlier in the pipeline. The freeze memorandum, issued on or within days of inauguration, directs agencies to send no new rule to the Office of the Federal Register until a department head appointed by the new president has reviewed it, to withdraw rules sent and awaiting publication, and to postpone, commonly by sixty days, the effective dates of rules published under the old administration and still pending. The third instrument belongs to Congress. The Congressional Review Act, enacted in 1996 and codified at 5 U.S.C. &sect;&sect;801–808, requires agencies to report each rule to both houses and gives Congress a window, sixty days of continuous session from receipt, to pass a joint resolution of disapproval in a text the statute itself dictates: “That Congress disapproves the rule submitted by the [agency] relating to [name of the rule], and such rule shall have no force or effect.” A rule disapproved is “treated as though such rule had never taken effect,” and the statute adds the provision with no parallel elsewhere in the reversal machinery: the rule “may not be reissued in substantially the same form” unless a later law authorizes it. Senate consideration runs on fast-track procedures without a filibuster. The fourth instrument is the quietest: the withdrawal of pending rules from the Unified Agenda of Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions, the government's semiannual inventory of work in progress, and the formal withdrawal notices agencies publish in the Federal Register when they abandon a proposed rule outright. Between the freeze and the withdrawal, an incoming administration can stop nearly everything its predecessor left unfinished, and the record shows each administration doing so.

The revocation counts

The American Presidency Project's comparison of the four party-changing transitions of this century counts executive orders only, through the first hundred days of each term, and the desk prints its figures with that scope attached. George W. Bush published eleven executive orders in the window and revoked five prior orders. Barack Obama published nineteen and revoked nine. Donald Trump published thirty-three in the first hundred days of 2017 and revoked thirteen. Joseph Biden published forty-two and revoked sixty-seven, with twenty-one of his orders carrying revocations inside them; across every category of presidential document in his first hundred days, the Project counts seventy-six prior orders explicitly rejected—revoked, amended, suspended, or reversed—in twenty-five of one hundred six documents. The unit of reversal then changed. Earlier presidents revoked predecessor orders inside orders of their own, a few at a time; the dedicated rescission order, a document whose whole content is a list of the dead, appears in the recent transitions. On January 20, 2021, Executive Order 13992 revoked six named regulatory orders of the Trump administration, including the two-for-one regulatory budget order of 2017, and a companion order the same day, Executive Order 13990, revoked nine further executive orders, three memoranda, and a pipeline permit on the American Presidency Project's reading of its text. Two further orders in February and May 2021, titled “Revocation of Certain Presidential Actions,” lengthened the list. On January 20, 2025, the instrument reached its present scale: Executive Order 14148 revoked seventy-eight presidential orders and memoranda of the Biden administration in Section 2, items (a) through the end of the alphabet twice over, and directed the president's domestic, economic, and national security advisers to compile lists of further candidates. The follow-up order of March 14, 2025, states the running total in its own first section—“I rescinded 78 Presidential orders and memoranda issued by then-President Biden”—and revoked eighteen additional actions, executive orders, national security memoranda, presidential memoranda, and determinations among them. Ninety-six bulk rescissions stand in the two orders within the administration's first eight weeks, ahead of the individual revocations carried in subject-matter orders across the same period.

The Congressional Review Act ledger

Congress's instrument slept for its first twenty years and then became routine. The Congressional Research Service's tally, which the George Washington University Regulatory Studies Center's cumulative count matches, records 461 resolutions of disapproval introduced between 1996 and 2024 and twenty enacted. The first success came on March 20, 2001, when the disapproval of the Labor Department's ergonomics rule, issued in the final months of the Clinton administration, became Public Law 107-5 under President Bush's signature. The second success waited sixteen years. In the 115th Congress of 2017–2018, sixteen disapprovals were enacted under President Trump's signature: the Regulatory Studies Center counts fifteen signed in 2017, fourteen of them against rules of the outgoing Obama administration, and Ballotpedia counts fourteen signed in the first four months alone. The sixteenth, signed May 21, 2018, disapproved a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau auto-lending guidance document, on the strength of a Government Accountability Office opinion holding that the guidance was a rule within the Act's meaning—the precedent that widened the instrument from rules to guidance. In the 117th Congress, three disapprovals were enacted under President Biden's signature, all on June 30, 2021: an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission conciliation rule, an Office of the Comptroller of the Currency “true lender” rule, and an Environmental Protection Agency rule that had itself rescinded the previous administration's methane standards, so that the disapproval restored the standards of two administrations back. The present Congress has exceeded the earlier record in a single session of work. The Regulatory Review's empirical analysis of the 2025 signings counts twenty-two disapproval resolutions signed into law during 2025, thirteen of them reaching rules submitted in the ordinary way during the statutory lookback window and nine reaching actions outside it: three California emissions waivers granted under the Clean Air Act, four Bureau of Land Management resource management plans, and further agency actions drawn in through Government Accountability Office opinions. The American Action Forum's tracker for the 119th Congress, in its update of October 26, 2026, counts twenty-three disapprovals enacted in the Congress and 148 resolutions introduced, addressing rules carrying an estimated $175.5 billion in compliance costs; the Senate majority leader's office, citing the same tracker as of November 2, 2026, records twenty-five resolutions passed and twenty-three become law. The desk prints the counts with their counters named, because the trackers differ at the edges over which agency actions count as rules, and the underlying statute's ledger—twenty enactments in twenty-eight years, then twenty-three in under two—is consistent on every count the desk reviewed.

Rules stopped in the pipeline

The freeze memorandum is the oldest of the four instruments in continuous use, and its documentary lineage is unbroken. President Reagan's memorandum postponing pending federal regulations issued on January 29, 1981, nine days into his term. The Clinton transition produced an Office of Management and Budget regulatory review memorandum published at 58 Federal Register 6074 on January 22, 1993. Thereafter the memorandum arrives on inauguration day itself, signed by the incoming chief of staff: Andrew Card's “Regulatory Review Plan” for President George W. Bush, published at 66 Federal Register 7702, dated January 20, 2001; Rahm Emanuel's “Regulatory Review” for President Obama, at 74 Federal Register 4435, dated January 20, 2009; Reince Priebus's “Regulatory Freeze Pending Review” for President Trump, dated January 20, 2017; and Ronald Klain's memorandum of the same title for President Biden, dated January 20, 2021. In 2025 the document rose a grade: the “Regulatory Freeze Pending Review” of January 20, 2025 issued as a presidential memorandum over President Trump's own signature. The one transition in the series without a freeze is 1989, when President George H. W. Bush succeeded a president of his own party and had, as the Davis Polk memorandum on the Priebus freeze records, little reason to block the publication of regulations developed under his predecessor's appointees. The language of the recent memoranda is near-identical across parties. The Priebus memorandum of 2017 and the Klain memorandum of 2021 open with the same sentence, word for word: “The President has asked me to communicate to each of you his plan for managing the Federal regulatory process at the outset of his Administration.” Each continues with the same purpose, in order to ensure that the President's appointees or designees have the opportunity to review any new or pending regulations; each directs that unpublished rules be withdrawn from the Office of the Federal Register; each postpones or asks agencies to postpone the effective dates of published rules by sixty days. What the freeze stops, the withdrawal finishes. On September 11, 2025, the Department of Justice published a single Federal Register notice withdrawing sixteen notices of proposed rulemaking, advance notices, and supplemental notices, together with thirty-eight further regulatory actions carried in the Unified Agenda, fifty-four items in one document, “as part of the Federal Government's deregulatory initiative.” Eleven days into the same administration, Executive Order 14192 of January 31, 2025 had set the arithmetic the withdrawals serve, directing that for each new regulation an agency issue, it identify ten existing regulations for repeal—the successor, at five times the rate, of the two-for-one order of 2017 that Executive Order 13992 had revoked in 2021.

Every era's reason

The justifications are filed inside the instruments, and they change vocabulary on the same schedule as the instruments change hands. The freeze memoranda justify themselves identically in every era, as a pause for review: the new president's appointees must have the opportunity to examine what the old president's appointees left in the pipeline, and the memoranda claim no larger warrant than the calendar. The revocation orders speak in the moral vocabulary of their administrations. President Biden's Executive Order 13992 of January 20, 2021 states its policy in its first section: “It is the policy of my Administration to use available tools to confront the urgent challenges facing the Nation, including the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, economic recovery, racial justice, and climate change,” and describes its own work in one clause—“This order revokes harmful policies and directives that threaten to frustrate the Federal Government's ability to confront these problems.” President Trump's Executive Order 14148 of January 20, 2025 opens its purpose section with the previous administration: “The previous administration has embedded deeply unpopular, inflationary, illegal, and radical practices within every agency and office of the Federal Government,” and continues, “Climate extremism has exploded inflation and overburdened businesses with regulation.” Its conclusion is filed as policy: “it is the policy of the United States to restore common sense to the Federal Government and unleash the potential of the American citizen,” and its promise is filed as a schedule: “The revocations within this order will be the first of many steps the United States Federal Government will take to repair our institutions and our economy.” The March 2025 order repeats the formula, describing its eighteen further rescissions as “necessary to advance the policy of the United States to restore common sense to the Federal Government and unleash the potential of American citizens.” Executive Order 14192 states the deregulatory program's purpose in the Department of Justice's quotation of it: “to promote prudent financial management and alleviate unnecessary regulatory burdens.” The Congressional Review Act states no reason at all; its stipulated resolution text names the agency and the rule and pronounces the rule without force or effect, and the reasons live in the floor debates instead. The desk notes the constant as a property of the documents: across forty-five years and five transitions, every instrument of reversal describes itself as repair—as review, restoration, or the removal of the harmful—and no instrument in the file describes its own operation as the substitution of one administration's preferences for another's, although a substitution is the entire content of each list.

The weather: prices and elections

The desk prints here two series from the record, side by side, and draws no line between them. The first is the Bureau of Labor Statistics' annual average change in the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers. In 1979 the index rose 11.3 percent; in 1980, 13.5 percent, the highest annual reading since 1947; in 1981, 10.3 percent. In the recent cycle the Bureau's table reads: 4.7 percent in 2021, 8.0 percent in 2022—the highest annual average since 1981, with the twelve-month rate reaching 9.1 percent in June 2022—then 4.1 percent in 2023, 2.9 percent in 2024, and 2.6 percent in 2025. The second series is the outcomes of the federal elections held in those years. On November 4, 1980, Governor Ronald Reagan defeated President Jimmy Carter; the presidency and the Senate changed parties, and the House remained with the president's party's opponents. On November 8, 2022, in the midterm elections of the high-inflation year, the House of Representatives changed parties and the Senate did not; the president's party gained one seat there. On November 5, 2024, former President Donald Trump defeated Vice President Kamala Harris; the presidency and the Senate changed parties, and the House remained with the incoming president's party. The reversal counts printed in this report belong to the administrations those elections and their successors seated: the freeze memorandum of January 1981 followed the election of 1980; the ergonomics disapproval of 2001 followed the election of 2000; the sixty-seven first-hundred-day revocations followed the election of 2020, held in a year when the index rose 1.2 percent; and the seventy-eight revocations of January 2025 followed the election of 2024. The desk files the two series in one section because they are the two halves of the public record on the subject, and it leaves their relation to the reader.

The standing first act

The record's forward entries show the instruments loaded in advance and still in use. Reversal is now announced before it can be executed: the American Presidency Project records that the Biden campaign published a set of “Day One” priorities before the inauguration of 2021 and that each had been addressed in orders on the first day; Ballotpedia's inventory of the Biden revocations records that the Trump campaign's 2024 agenda named the reissue of a revoked 2020 personnel order as a day-one priority of the next administration, and the order was among those the new administration issued on its return. The current administration's rescissions continued past the spring: on November 28, 2025, the president announced on social media that any document signed by his predecessor with an autopen, “which was approximately 92% of them, is hereby terminated, and of no further force or effect.” The 92 percent figure is the president's own; no White House record of signing methods supports it in the material the desk reviewed, and the desk found no single instrument in the Federal Register effecting the blanket termination the post announced—the declaration stands in the record as a statement of intent, filed outside the four instruments this report has tracked. Congress's instrument, meanwhile, is pre-loaded against the present administration by the statute's own design. The Congressional Review Act's lookback provision restarts the full disapproval window in a new session of Congress for rules submitted in the final sixty legislative days of the old one, and the Congressional Research Service's overview notes the provision “may hold particular import in years in which there is a change in party control of the presidency.” Rules the agencies submit in the closing weeks of the 119th Congress will accordingly arrive in the 120th as fresh targets, with their sixty days unspent, whoever holds the majority that receives them. The 148 resolutions of disapproval introduced in the present Congress, against the twenty-three enacted, mark the volume of the attempt on the record.

The record as it stands on November 14, 2026, is therefore this. Four instruments carry the whole of presidential reversal: the revocation clause, used five times against prior orders in the first hundred days of 2001 and sixty-seven times in the first hundred days of 2021, and seventy-eight times in a single order on January 20, 2025; the freeze memorandum, issued in near-identical language at every party-changing transition since 1981 and signed by the president himself in 2025; the Congressional Review Act disapproval, enacted once in the Act's first twenty years, sixteen times in 2017–2018, three times in 2021, and twenty-three times in the 119th Congress; and the withdrawal of pending rules, executed through the semiannual Unified Agenda and in Federal Register withdrawal notices—in one Justice Department notice of September 11, 2025, by fifty-four items at a stroke. Every instrument carries its justification in its own text, and the justifications agree in form across the parties that wield them: review, restoration, repair. The elections of the high-inflation years, 1980 and 2024, seated the administrations that then executed the two largest reversal programs in the file, and the desk prints that adjacency as record. The window for the next reversal is already open in the statute, and the practice the instruments serve—an incoming government striking the outgoing government's work as its first official act—stands in the record as routine, documented, and expected by both parties in turn.

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—the desk is filing it, not endorsing it—and each is described in plain terms: what it is and what it says. 13 items.

SubjectiveExecutive Order 14148, “Initial Rescissions of Harmful Executive Orders and Actions,” January 20, 2025—Federal Register, Vol. 90, p. 8237 (regulations.justia.com)
The order as printed in the Federal Register: a purpose section charging the previous administration with embedding “deeply unpopular, inflationary, illegal, and radical practices” in every agency, and a Section 2 revoking the listed executive actions of the Biden administration item by item—the list the administration's March order later totals at seventy-eight. The order.

SubjectiveExecutive Order 14236, “Additional Rescissions of Harmful Executive Orders and Actions,” March 14, 2025—Compilation of Presidential Documents (govinfo.gov)
The second bulk rescission order: its purpose section states that the January order rescinded seventy-eight presidential orders and memoranda, and its Section 2 revokes eighteen further actions—executive orders, national security memoranda, presidential memoranda, determinations, and a waiver—dated from January 2021 to September 2024. The order.

SubjectiveExecutive Order 13992, “Revocation of Certain Executive Orders Concerning Federal Regulation,” January 20, 2021—Federal Register, Vol. 86, p. 7049 (govinfo.gov)
President Biden's first-day revocation order in its Federal Register printing: the policy section naming the pandemic, economic recovery, racial justice, and climate change, and Section 2 revoking six of the previous administration's regulatory orders, including the two-for-one regulatory budget order and the guidance-document orders. The order.

SubjectiveThe American Presidency Project—“Biden in Action: the First 100 Days” (presidency.ucsb.edu)
The Project's comparative count of early executive action across the four party-changing transitions of the century: executive orders published, orders carrying revocations, and prior orders revoked in the first hundred days—five under Bush in 2001, nine under Obama in 2009, thirteen under Trump in 2017, sixty-seven under Biden in 2021—with its wider count of seventy-six prior orders rejected across all presidential documents in Biden's first hundred days. The analysis.

SubjectiveRonald A. Klain, “Regulatory Freeze Pending Review,” memorandum of January 20, 2021 (bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov)
The Biden chief of staff's first-day freeze memorandum: no rule to be proposed or issued until a department head appointed after noon on January 20, 2021 has approved it, rules sent to the Federal Register and unpublished to be withdrawn, and effective dates of published rules to be postponed for review. The memorandum.

SubjectiveReince Priebus, “Regulatory Freeze Pending Review,” memorandum of January 20, 2017 (trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov)
The Trump chief of staff's first-day freeze memorandum, in the same opening words as its 2021 successor: no regulation to be sent to the Office of the Federal Register until a president-appointed department head reviews and approves it, unpublished regulations withdrawn, and effective dates postponed sixty days—extended, in its departure from precedent, to guidance documents. The memorandum.

SubjectiveDavis Polk & Wardwell—client memorandum on the Priebus freeze, January 21, 2017 (davispolk.com)
A law firm's comparison of the 2017 freeze against its predecessors, with the documentary lineage in its footnote: the Reagan memorandum of January 29, 1981, the Clinton review of January 22, 1993, the Card memorandum at 66 Federal Register 7702, and the Emanuel memorandum at 74 Federal Register 4435—and its note that the same-party transition of 1989 is the exception in the series. The memorandum.

SubjectiveCongressional Research Service—“The Congressional Review Act (CRA): A Brief Overview,” updated August 29, 2024 (congress.gov)
CRS's account of the Act: the stipulated text of a disapproval resolution, the rule treated as though it had never taken effect, the bar on reissue in substantially the same form, the lookback provision for rules submitted near adjournment, and the tally of twenty rules overturned—one in the 107th Congress, sixteen in the 115th, three in the 117th. The overview.

SubjectiveGeorge Washington University Regulatory Studies Center—“President Trump's State of the Union Claim on Regulation: The 2017 Data Are In,” February 1, 2018 (regulatorystudies.columbian.gwu.edu)
The Center's count of the 2017 Congressional Review Act season: fifteen resolutions of disapproval signed in 2017, fourteen of them nullifying rules of the outgoing administration, against the single prior success in the Act's history—the 2001 disapproval of the Clinton administration's ergonomics rule. The analysis.

SubjectiveBallotpedia News—“Biden signs three Congressional Review Act bills repealing Trump-era rules,” July 2, 2021 (news.ballotpedia.org)
News reporting of the June 30, 2021 signings: the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission conciliation rule, the Comptroller of the Currency “true lender” rule, and the Environmental Protection Agency methane rule disapproved in one ceremony, bringing the Act's total of repealed rules to twenty. The report.

SubjectiveThe Regulatory Review—“The Weaponization of the Congressional Review Act in 2025,” February 3, 2026 (theregreview.org)
An empirical analysis of all disapproval resolutions signed into law in 2025: twenty-two in the calendar year, thirteen reaching rules submitted in the ordinary lookback manner and nine reaching actions beyond it, among them three California Clean Air Act waivers and four Bureau of Land Management resource management plans; eighteen of the twenty-two concerned environmental matters. The analysis.

SubjectiveAmerican Action Forum—Congressional Review Act tracker for the 119th Congress, as reported October 26, 2026 (americanactionforum.org)
The Forum's running tally of the present Congress: 148 resolutions of disapproval introduced, addressing rules with an estimated $175.5 billion in compliance costs, and twenty-three passed into law repealing rules of the previous administration. The Senate majority leader's office, citing the same tracker as of November 2, 2026, records twenty-five resolutions passed. The tracker report.

SubjectiveU.S. Department of Justice—“Withdrawal of Rulemaking Actions,” Federal Register notice, September 11, 2025 (federalregister.gov); U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics—annual Consumer Price Index table (bls.gov)
Two primary documents filed together. The Justice Department's notice withdraws sixteen published proposed rules and thirty-eight Unified Agenda actions, fifty-four items, as part of the government's deregulatory initiative under Executive Order 14192. The Bureau of Labor Statistics' table gives the annual average change in consumer prices: 4.7 percent in 2021, 8.0 percent in 2022, 4.1 percent in 2023, 2.9 percent in 2024, and 2.6 percent in 2025. The withdrawal notice; the price table.

### Free Speech: What the Record Shows About What the First Amendment Protects, and What Other Democracies Do Instead

Filed as: Special Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-14T10:55:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-14-free-speech-record.html

Special Report

The First Amendment · The State-Action Line · The Pandemic Files · Article 10 · The Basic Law · The Funding Lever

Objective

Free Speech: What the Record Shows About What the First Amendment Protects, and What Other Democracies Do Instead

United States law protects speech that is hateful, offensive, and Nazi in content, and forbids the government to act against it directly, indirectly, or through pressure on the private companies that carry it; the record runs from the Sedition Act of 1798 to Brandenburg, to the Murthy litigation over pandemic-era pressure on platforms, to a September 2025 letter in which Alphabet told Congress that administration officials pressed it to remove content that broke none of its rules. The other democracies write the limit into the right itself: Britain recorded 12,183 arrests in 2023 under two communications statutes and jailed a woman for 31 months for one post; Germany's Basic Law subordinates expression to the general laws, bans whole categories of symbols, and sent police to search a pensioner's home over a meme; Canada sustains a hate-propaganda law under its Charter's limits clause. In November 2026 the American line is being tested at Rutgers, where a public university has declined to cancel a former Border Patrol commander's speech, and in the federal courts, where the funding lever the government used against Harvard has been held unconstitutional retaliation and the appeal is pending.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1055 ET, Saturday, November 14, 2026.

Two documents describe the American settlement on speech, and both are short. The first is the First Amendment, ratified December 15, 1791: “Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press.” The second is the sentence with which Justice Alito closed the Supreme Court's unanimous judgment in Matal v. Tam in 2017: “Speech that demeans on the basis of race, ethnicity, gender, religion, age, disability, or any other similar ground is hateful; but the proudest boast of our free speech jurisprudence is that we protect the freedom to express ‘the thought that we hate.’” Between the text and that sentence stands the whole of the record this report prints: what the amendment forbids, what it permits, the narrow categories it leaves outside, the line it draws at the government's own hand—including the hand applied indirectly, through threats, through pressure on private platforms, and through money—and the contrasting settlements of the other democracies, in which expression is a qualified right, balanced in the text itself against dignity, reputation, and public order, and enforced against posts, memes, and T-shirts by arrest and imprisonment. The comparison is between two legal architectures: one in which the limit sits outside the right, in a short list of harms the courts police case by case, and one in which the limit is written into the right's own text, where legislatures and police apply it in advance.

The spine: from the Sedition Act to Brandenburg

The American law of speech began with a prosecution statute. The Sedition Act of 1798 made it a crime to publish “false, scandalous and malicious writing” against the government, Congress, or the President; some twenty-five people were arrested under it and ten convicted, including a sitting congressman, before the act expired on March 3, 1801, and President Jefferson pardoned those convicted. No court struck it down; its repudiation came through elections and pardons, and the Supreme Court noted in 1964 that the attack upon its validity “has carried the day in the court of history.” The modern doctrine arrived in stages. In Schenck v. United States (1919), Justice Holmes upheld Espionage Act convictions and gave the law its first test—whether words create a “clear and present danger” of evils Congress may prevent—and eight months later, dissenting in Abrams v. United States, he stated the theory the test would eventually serve: “the best test of truth is the power of the thought to get itself accepted in the competition of the market.” In Gitlow v. New York (1925), the Court assumed that freedom of speech is among the liberties the Fourteenth Amendment protects against the states, binding Albany as the First Amendment binds Congress. The endpoint of the line came in Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969), which set the standard that still governs advocacy of force or illegality: the state may not forbid advocacy “except where such advocacy is directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action and is likely to incite or produce such action.” A Ku Klux Klan leader's filmed threats of “revengeance” against the government did not meet it. The distance between 1798 and 1969 is the distance between punishing scandalous writing about the President and protecting a Klansman's rally speech; the doctrine traveled it in one direction only, each generation's test narrower than the last.

What the law does not protect

The unprotected categories are few, defined, and printed in the cases. Incitement is the Brandenburg category above: intent, imminence, and likelihood, all three required. True threats are outside the amendment; in Counterman v. Colorado (2023), the Court held that the state must prove at least recklessness—that the speaker “consciously disregarded a substantial risk” that the words would be taken as threatening violence—before a statement may be punished as a threat. Obscenity is governed by Miller v. California (1973) and its three-part test, a category confined to sexual material and separate from offensiveness as such. Defamation of a public official requires proof of “actual malice”—knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth—under New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964), the case that constitutionalized the law of libel out of a segregationist commissioner's suit over a civil-rights advertisement. Fraud and speech integral to criminal conduct—solicitation, conspiracy, perjury, extortion—are punishable as the conduct they are part of. Beyond that list, the Court has refused to go: in United States v. Stevens (2010) and Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association (2011) it declined to create new unprotected categories for depictions of animal cruelty and for violent video games sold to minors, holding that the existing categories are a closed historical set, not a balancing test to be extended by analogy. The categories share a property the desk records because the comparison below turns on it: each is defined by a harm the speech does—imminent violence, a credible threat, a lie that damages—and none is defined by the offensiveness of what the speech says.

What it protects, hate included

There is no hate-speech exception in American law, and the record of its rejection is repeated and recent. In R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul (1992), the Court struck down an ordinance that punished cross-burning and other displays that arouse “anger, alarm or resentment” on the basis of race, color, creed, religion, or gender: even within the punishable class of fighting words, the government may not select the racist instances for special prohibition. In Snyder v. Phelps (2011), the Court held 8–1 that a fringe church's picketing of a Marine's funeral with signs reading “Thank God for Dead Soldiers” was speech on matters of public concern, protected against a tort judgment for emotional distress. In Matal v. Tam (2017), a unanimous Court struck down the federal trademark law's disparagement clause, holding that a statute punishing speech that demeans is viewpoint discrimination, and printing the sentence quoted in this report's first paragraph. The older test of the same principle is the Skokie litigation of 1977–78: when the National Socialist Party of America announced a march in Skokie, Illinois, a village with a large population of Holocaust survivors, the village enacted ordinances against military-style uniforms, racially slurring literature, and demonstrations promoting racial hatred. The Supreme Court's per curiam order in National Socialist Party of America v. Village of Skokie (1977) required immediate appellate review of the injunction against the march, and the Illinois courts struck the ordinances down; the party in the end marched in Chicago in June 1978. Nazi uniform, Nazi literature, and Nazi slogans, displayed by actual Nazis in a town of survivors, are the historical center of the American doctrine: the speech was protected not because any court valued it, but because the categories contain no entry for it.

The state-action line, and this week's test of it

The amendment binds the government. It does not bind a private platform, a private employer, or a counter-demonstrator, and the courts police the boundary in both directions: private suppression is lawful, government evasion of the boundary is not. The evasion doctrine is old. In Bantam Books, Inc. v. Sullivan (1963), the Court held that a state commission's letters to distributors—identifying objectionable books, reminding recipients of the commission's duty to recommend prosecutions, followed by police visits—were state action suppressing speech, although the commission had no power to ban anything itself. The Court restated the principle unanimously in National Rifle Association of America v. Vullo (2024): “Government officials cannot attempt to coerce private parties in order to punish or suppress views that the government disfavors,” and a financial regulator's pressure on insurers to drop a disfavored advocacy group states a First Amendment claim. On the boundary's other side stands the heckler's veto. In Terminiello v. Chicago (1949), the Court reversed the breach-of-peace conviction of a speaker whose address had drawn a violent crowd outside the hall: “a function of free speech under our system of government is to invite dispute.” In Forsyth County v. Nationalist Movement (1992), it struck down a permit fee set by officials according to the expected cost of controlling hostile listeners. The crowd's anger is not a charge the speaker pays, and the crowd's own speech—protest, denunciation, counter-demonstration—is protected on the same terms as the speaker's.

The line runs through the public campus in a specific way, because a public university is the government. In Healy v. James (1972), the Court held that a state college may not refuse recognition to a student organization because it disapproves of the group's views; in Widmar v. Vincent (1981), that a university which opens its facilities to student groups may not close them to a religious group on content grounds. A recognized student organization invites a speaker with its own funds and standing; the university that cancels or burdens the event because of the speaker's content acts as the state suppressing speech, and the students who protest the event exercise the same right in the opposite direction. The distinction is not a courtesy. It is the whole doctrine in one room.

The room, this week, is at Rutgers. NJ.com reported on November 12, 2026 that the Rutgers College Republicans, a recognized student organization at Rutgers University—New Brunswick, the state's public university, have invited Gregory Bovino, the former commander-at-large of the U.S. Border Patrol who directed the administration's urban immigration operations, to speak on Monday, November 16, from 6 to 8 p.m. in Trayes Hall at the Douglass Student Center, with audience questions to follow. A petition organized by the Climate Revolution Action Network, demanding that the university cancel the event, had gathered more than 1,600 signatures when NJ.com reported and nearly 2,000 by November 13; its text states that Bovino's presence “raises serious concerns about the safety and well-being of the Rutgers community” and risks “creating an intimidating and hostile environment for Rutgers students.” Community organizations announced a press conference and demonstration outside the venue an hour before the event. NJ.com's headline carried the protesters' formulation: “We don't stand for Nazis.” As of this filing, the university has taken no action against the event: it has declined to cancel it, and it has said it will provide a designated area for counter-protesters. The event is scheduled, not yet held; its outcome is not in the record. What is in the record is the alignment of the parties with the doctrine printed above—the invitation issued by a student organization, the cancellation demanded of the state institution, the institution declining, and the protest planned as speech against speech. Any change in the university's position would move the case from the protesters' column of the ledger to the government's.

The pandemic record: pressure, in documents

During the pandemic years the boundary question moved from distributors and insurers to the platforms that carry most public speech, and the record of what passed between the government and those platforms is unusually documentary. Beginning December 2, 2022, the new owner of Twitter released internal company records to journalists, published in installments as the Twitter Files: they showed federal agencies and officials flagging specific accounts and posts for the company's attention, the company's internal debate over suppressing the New York Post's October 2020 reporting on Hunter Biden's laptop, and a Stanford-based project that reported true and misleading posts alike to platform partners. The administration's own institutional attempt was brief: the Department of Homeland Security announced a Disinformation Governance Board on April 27, 2022, paused it within three weeks, and dissolved it on August 24, 2022. The litigation record is the spine. Missouri and Louisiana, with individual plaintiffs, sued in 2022, alleging that federal officials had coerced and significantly encouraged platforms to suppress disfavored viewpoints, including on the pandemic and the 2020 election. A district court entered a preliminary injunction on July 4, 2023. The Fifth Circuit, on September 8, 2023, narrowed it but sustained its core: the White House, the Surgeon General's office, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the court found, had likely coerced or significantly encouraged the platforms' moderation decisions; other agencies were removed for want of comparable proof. The Supreme Court, on June 26, 2024, in Murthy v. Missouri, held 6–3 that the plaintiffs lacked standing, because the chain between the officials' communications and the platforms' independent decisions was not traceable on the record as presented. The Court reached no other question: the merits were not decided, and the Fifth Circuit's findings stand vacated with the injunction, without adoption or rejection by the higher court. The documentary record and the legal record therefore say different things, and the desk prints both: the communications happened, in volume, as the letters below attest; whether they crossed the constitutional line the Vullo case draws has never been adjudicated on a full record.

Two letters from the companies themselves close the file. On August 26, 2024, Meta's chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, wrote to the chairman of the House Judiciary Committee: “In 2021, senior officials from the Biden Administration, including the White House, repeatedly pressured our teams for months to censor certain COVID-19 content, including humor and satire, and expressed a lot of frustration with our teams when we didn't agree.” The letter states the boundary as the company drew it in the same paragraph: “Ultimately, it was our decision whether or not to take content down, and we own our decisions, including COVID-19-related changes we made to our enforcement in the wake of this pressure. I believe the government pressure was wrong, and I regret that we were not more outspoken about it.” On September 23, 2025, counsel for Alphabet, YouTube's parent, wrote to the same committee in materially stronger terms: “Senior Biden Administration officials, including White House officials, conducted repeated and sustained outreach to Alphabet and pressed the Company regarding certain user-generated content related to the COVID-19 pandemic that did not violate its policies.” The letter states that the administration “created a political atmosphere that sought to influence the actions of platforms based on their concerns regarding misinformation,” that government attempts to dictate moderation are “unacceptable and wrong,” and it commits the company to offer reinstatement to every creator terminated under its retired COVID-19 and election-integrity policies. The committee's ranking member answered the same day that the letter had “the ring of a false and coerced confession” extracted by the current majority's own pressure on the company, and noted that Alphabet employees had testified under oath that they were not coerced. Both letters, and the objection to the second, are part of the record; the pressure each describes ran from the government of the day toward the platform, and the pressure alleged against the second letter's production ran from the government of the next day toward the same platform. The doctrine of Bantam Books and Vullo does not distinguish between administrations, and neither does this report.

The lever in the statute book

The platforms' exposure to pressure has a statutory address. Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996, codified at 47 U.S.C. &sect; 230, provides that “no provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the publisher or speaker of any information provided by another information content provider,” and separately protects good-faith moderation. The provision is the legal foundation of the platforms' business: without it, carrying third-party speech at scale carries a publisher's liability for it. Its repeal has been invoked by officials of both parties in disputes over moderation. President Biden, as a candidate, told the New York Times editorial board in January 2020 that Section 230 “immediately should be revoked.” President Trump, on May 28, 2020, after a platform labeled his posts, signed Executive Order 13925, directing agencies to construe the statute narrowly and to review federal advertising on platforms; the order was revoked by his successor in May 2021. The record shows the statute functioning in these episodes as the consideration in the room: the companies' immunity is a grant of Congress, both parties' leaders have placed its withdrawal on the table while disputing the companies' moderation, and the companies' letters record the resulting atmosphere in their own words. No finding in the record ties a specific removal to a specific threat about Section 230; the desk prints the sequence, the documents, and the absence, together.

Three other democracies, statute by statute

The United Kingdom. Britain has no First Amendment. The right it has is Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, carried into domestic law by the Human Rights Act 1998, and Article 10 is a qualified right on its face: after guaranteeing freedom of expression, its second paragraph provides that the right “may be subject to such formalities, conditions, restrictions or penalties as are prescribed by law and are necessary in a democratic society, in the interests of national security, territorial integrity or public safety, for the prevention of disorder or crime, for the protection of health or morals, for the protection of the reputation or rights of others.” The statutes that do the work are ordinary criminal law. Section 127 of the Communications Act 2003 makes it an offence to send, over a public electronic communications network, “a message or other matter that is grossly offensive or of an indecent, obscene or menacing character.” Section 1 of the Malicious Communications Act 1988 covers matter that is indecent or grossly offensive sent with intent to cause distress or anxiety. The Times, compiling freedom-of-information returns in an investigation published in April 2025, counted 12,183 arrests under the two statutes in 2023 by the forces of England and Wales that answered—about thirty-three a day, up from 7,734 in 2019—and Ministry of Justice figures reported alongside the count show fewer than one in ten of those arrested in 2023, some 1,119 people, were sentenced. The figures are arrests, not convictions; no American counterpart figure exists, because no American statute makes a grossly offensive message as such a crime. Alongside the statutes stand the non-crime hate incidents: since 2014, police guidance has required the recording of incidents perceived by the victim or any other person to be motivated by hostility to a protected characteristic, where no crime is alleged; the Court of Appeal held in the Miller case in December 2021 that the guidance's recording regime unlawfully interfered with Article 10 rights. A joint review by the College of Policing and the National Police Chiefs' Council concluded in March 2026 that the system is not fit for purpose, and the government accepted recommendations to end the recording of non-crime hate incidents; the replacement framework is expected in early 2027, and the existing arrangements remain in force until it arrives. The individual case the record is known by is Lucy Connolly, a childminder of Northampton and the wife of a Conservative councillor. On July 29, 2024, the day three girls were murdered at a dance class in Southport, she posted on X: “Mass deportation now, set fire to all the f****** hotels full of the b******* for all I care&hellip; if that makes me racist so be it.” The post was viewed some 310,000 times before she deleted it within hours. She pleaded guilty to publishing material with intent to stir up racial hatred, under the Public Order Act 1986, and on October 17, 2024 was sentenced at Birmingham Crown Court to thirty-one months' imprisonment, forty percent to be served in custody. The Court of Appeal refused her appeal against sentence in May 2025; she was released on licence in August 2025, having served about twelve and a half months including remand. Her sentence sits inside the American categories at no point: the post advocated violence against property and persons in terms the Brandenburg test would measure by imminence and likelihood, and it was punished instead for the hatred it intended to stir.

Germany. Article 5 of the Basic Law guarantees freedom of expression, of the press, and of broadcasting, and qualifies the guarantee in its second paragraph: “These rights shall find their limits in the provisions of general laws, in provisions for the protection of young persons, and in the right to personal honour.” The general laws include the criminal code's speech offences. Section 86a of the Criminal Code punishes the display of symbols of unconstitutional organizations—the swastika above all—with up to three years' imprisonment, subject to exceptions for art, scholarship, teaching, and reporting; a swastika on a T-shirt worn in public is a criminal matter in Germany, where the same shirt in the United States is the Skokie record. Section 130 punishes incitement to hatred against segments of the population. Section 188, expanded in 2021, gives persons in political life enhanced protection against insult and defamation; police statistics reported in 2026 counted 4,792 investigations under the provision in 2025, a record. The NetzDG—the Network Enforcement Act of 2017—obliged platforms to remove manifestly unlawful content within twenty-four hours on pain of fines up to &euro;50 million, until the statute was largely superseded by the European Union's Digital Services Act in 2024. The enforcement case that made the system legible abroad began on November 12, 2024, when Bavarian police searched the home of Stefan Niehoff, a 64-year-old retired soldier, in the early morning and confiscated his tablet, after he reposted a meme describing the vice chancellor and economics minister, Robert Habeck, as a “Schwachkopf”—a professional moron—in a parody of a shampoo advertisement. The search followed a criminal complaint in a system in which a state reporting office had registered the post and forwarded it to the police. The insult proceedings were later dropped, prosecutors concluding the insult lacked the weight the statute requires. The search itself was lawful, warrant-backed, and unremarkable under the governing texts: that is the datum.

Canada. Section 2(b) of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees “freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication,” and section 1 subjects every Charter right to “such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.” In R. v. Keegstra (1990), the Supreme Court of Canada upheld, 4–3, the Criminal Code's prohibition on the wilful promotion of hatred, under which a teacher had been convicted for teaching his students antisemitic doctrine: the limit was demonstrably justified, the majority held, by the harm hate propaganda does to its targets and to the society the Charter constitutes. The Canadian settlement is the British and German settlements' sibling: the right is real, and its limit is internal, applied by balancing at the point of legislation and sustained by the courts as a feature of the constitutional text rather than a violation of it.

The factual burden of the comparison can now be stated without emphasis. In the United States, expression is limited by a closed list of harm categories, construed by courts, and hateful content as such appears in none of them; in the United Kingdom, Germany, and Canada, the governing texts qualify the right in advance, and the official category of unlawful speech includes speech whose offence is the hatred, offence, or insult it expresses. American officials describing the European enforcement and European officials defending it use the same words for the two systems and mean different things by them, because the instruments differ. When Vice President Vance addressed the Munich Security Conference on February 14, 2025, he named the difference from the American side: “What I worry about is the threat from within. The retreat of Europe from some of its most fundamental values: values shared with the United States of America.” He cited Brussels, where, he said, “EU commissars warn citizens that they intend to shut down social media during times of civil unrest the moment they spot what they've judged to be, quote, ‘hateful content,’” and he stated the American premise as a rule of democracy: “dismissing people, dismissing their concerns or worse yet, shutting down media, shutting down elections or shutting people out of the political process protects nothing.” European leaders, including Finland's president and Germany's chancellor, rejected the characterization and defended their jurisdictions' authority to regulate hate speech and disinformation. The disagreement is genuine and the instruments are as printed. Each side's description of the other's system is, on the documents, substantially accurate; what differs is the settlement each text embodies about where the limit on expression is allowed to sit.

The money lever, 2025–2026

The current administration's instrument toward universities has been neither prosecution nor injunction but money. Its stated rationale, repeated across the 2025 funding actions, is the enforcement of federal anti-discrimination law: that universities receiving federal funds permitted antisemitic harassment after October 7, 2023, in violation of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, and that federal research money may be withdrawn from institutions out of compliance. In March 2025 the government cancelled some $400 million in Columbia University's grants and contracts on that ground. Columbia settled. Under the agreement of July 23, 2025, the university pays $200 million to the federal government over three years and $21 million to settle Equal Employment Opportunity Commission investigations; the government reinstated the vast majority of the terminated grants and restored the university's eligibility for future funding; a jointly selected independent monitor oversees implementation; and Columbia states, and the agreement provides, that the university retains authority over faculty hiring, admissions, and academic decision-making, and admits no liability. The Secretary of Education said the government hoped the agreement would serve as a template for other universities. Harvard University declined the administration's April 2025 demands; some $2.2 billion in its research funding was frozen and grants terminated. Harvard sued, and on September 3, 2025, Judge Allison D. Burroughs of the District of Massachusetts held for the university: the freeze and terminations, she ruled, violated the First Amendment as retaliation for protected speech and as unconstitutional conditions and coercion, and violated Title VI's procedures and the Administrative Procedure Act besides; the freeze orders were vacated and the government permanently enjoined from reimposing them on the reasoning used. The opinion's conclusion contains the sentence by which it is known: on the record before her, she wrote, it was “difficult to conclude anything other than that Defendants used antisemitism as a smokescreen for a targeted, ideologically-motivated assault” on the nation's premier universities. The government appealed on December 31, 2025; the First Circuit heard argument on October 5, 2026, and, as of this filing, has not decided. Research payments to Harvard have resumed under the district court's order while the appeal pends. The two outcomes stand side by side in the record and the desk draws no line between them: one university purchased the restoration of its funding at the settlement table, accepting a monitor and policy commitments; the other obtained restoration from a court, on the ground that the government's use of the funding lever against a university's speech and governance is the indirect action the First Amendment forbids. Whether the appellate court sustains that ground is the largest open question in the American speech record as this report files.

The timeline

1791 — The First Amendment is ratified as part of the Bill of Rights. 1798 — The Sedition Act criminalizes scandalous writing against the government; it expires in 1801 unrepealed by any court. 1919 — Schenck states the clear-and-present-danger test; Holmes's Abrams dissent states the market theory. 1925 — Gitlow binds the states. 1949 — Terminiello reverses a speaker's conviction won by a hostile crowd. 1963 — Bantam Books holds informal official pressure to be state action. 1964 — Sullivan constitutionalizes libel. 1969 — Brandenburg sets the incitement standard that still governs. 1972–81 — Healy and Widmar carry the doctrine onto the public campus. 1977–78 — The Skokie litigation protects a Nazi march. 1990 — Canada's Keegstra sustains a hate-propaganda law under the Charter's limits clause. 1992 — R.A.V. and Forsyth County reject hate-speech selection and the heckler's fee. 1996 — Section 230 is enacted. 2011 — Snyder v. Phelps protects funeral picketing. 2017 — Matal v. Tam prints the doctrine's boast; Germany enacts the NetzDG. 2020 — Candidate Biden says Section 230 should be revoked; President Trump signs Executive Order 13925. 2022 — The Disinformation Governance Board is announced in April and dissolved in August; the Twitter Files begin in December; Missouri's suit proceeds. 2023 — Counterman sets the recklessness standard for true threats; the Fifth Circuit sustains the core of the coercion findings against four federal actors; British police make 12,183 arrests under the communications statutes. 2024 — Vullo restates the coercion doctrine unanimously; Murthy disposes of the platform case on standing; Zuckerberg's letter in August; Connolly sentenced in October; the Niehoff search in November. 2025 — Vance at Munich in February; Columbia settles in July; Burroughs rules for Harvard in September; Alphabet's letter in September; the government appeals the Harvard judgment in December. 2026 — Britain's police bodies declare the non-crime hate incident system unfit in March, replacement due in 2027; the First Circuit hears the Harvard appeal in October; Rutgers declines to cancel the Bovino event in November, and the event stands scheduled for November 16.

The record as it stands on November 14, 2026, is therefore this. The American text of 1791 and the case law built on it protect expression that the other democracies punish, including expression that is hateful, Nazi in content, and aimed at the bereaved, and they forbid the government four roads to the same end: direct prohibition outside the harm categories, selection among viewpoints within them, coercion of the private parties who carry speech, and—on the one appellate-pending ruling in the file—retaliation through federal money. The pandemic file shows the third road traveled in volume and adjudicated nowhere: the communications are documented, the companies' letters are on congressional paper, and the only Supreme Court disposition is on standing. The European and Canadian files show the alternative architecture operating as designed, at volumes the documents state plainly—12,183 British arrests in a year under two communications statutes, a thirty-one-month sentence for one post, 4,792 German investigations in a year into insults against politicians, a pensioner's home searched at dawn over a meme, and a Canadian hate-propaganda law sustained by the Charter's own limits clause. On Monday a former Border Patrol commander is scheduled to speak at a public university in New Jersey because the state institution that owns the room has declined to stop him, while protesters prepare to answer him in the street outside—the two protected acts facing each other across the state-action line, which is where the American record, from the Sedition Act forward, has always located them.

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—the desk is filing it, not endorsing it—and each is described in plain terms: what it is and what it says. 15 items.

SubjectiveNational Archives—the Bill of Rights, transcript (archives.gov)
The engrossed text of the amendments ratified December 15, 1791, including the First Amendment in full: religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition in a single sentence addressed to Congress. The transcript.

SubjectiveU.S. Supreme Court—Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U.S. 444 (1969), opinion text (law.cornell.edu)
The per curiam opinion setting the incitement standard that still governs advocacy of force or lawlessness: protected unless directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it. The defendant was an Ohio Ku Klux Klan leader filmed at a rally. The opinion.

SubjectiveU.S. Supreme Court—Matal v. Tam, 582 U.S. 218 (2017), opinion text (law.cornell.edu)
Justice Alito's opinion for a unanimous Court striking down the trademark disparagement clause as viewpoint discrimination, closing with the statement that the proudest boast of American free-speech jurisprudence is protecting the freedom to express the thought that we hate. The opinion.

SubjectiveU.S. Supreme Court—Murthy v. Missouri, docket 23-411 (supremecourt.gov)
The Court's docket in the platform-pressure case: the June 26, 2024 judgment holding, 6–3, that the state and individual plaintiffs lacked standing, and the filings through which the Fifth Circuit's coercion findings came up and were vacated without a merits ruling. The docket.

SubjectiveMeta Platforms—letter of Mark Zuckerberg to Chairman Jim Jordan, August 26, 2024 (reproduced at socialmediatoday.com)
The letter in full: senior Biden administration officials, including the White House, repeatedly pressured Meta's teams for months in 2021 to censor COVID-19 content including humor and satire; the decisions were ultimately Meta's and it owns them; the pressure was wrong and the company regrets not being more outspoken. The letter and report.

SubjectiveKing & Spalding, counsel for Alphabet Inc.—statement of facts to the House Judiciary Committee, September 23, 2025 (docs.reclaimthenet.org)
Alphabet's letter to Chairman Jordan, delivered under subpoena: senior Biden administration officials conducted repeated and sustained outreach and pressed the company over COVID-19 content that did not violate its policies; the administration created a political atmosphere to influence platform actions; government dictation of moderation is unacceptable and wrong; and YouTube will offer reinstatement to all creators terminated under its retired COVID-19 and election-integrity policies. The letter.

SubjectiveU.S. House Judiciary Committee Democrats—statement of Ranking Member Jamie Raskin, September 23, 2025 (democrats-judiciary.house.gov)
The ranking member's answer to the Alphabet letter the day it arrived: that it has the ring of a false and coerced confession, that twenty Alphabet witnesses testified under penalty of perjury that they were not coerced by the Biden administration, and that the committee majority has declined to release the transcripts. The statement.

SubjectiveNJ Advance Media—“N.J. students revolt over ‘fascist’ event with ex-ICE leader. ‘We don’t stand for Nazis,’” November 12, 2026 (nj.com, reported by Brianna Kudisch)
The news report of the Rutgers College Republicans' invitation to former Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino for November 16, the petition demanding the university cancel the event, and the planned protest. The Record's opinion desk carried the companion argument under the headline “Greg Bovino is odious. He should still speak at Rutgers,” recording that the university has resisted calls to block the appearance and will provide a designated area for counter-protesters. The column.

SubjectiveNational Day Laborer Organizing Network—“Community Slams Rutgers for Rolling Out Red Carpet for Greg Bovino,” November 10, 2026 (ndlon.org)
The organizing coalition's own statement: a community press conference outside the Douglass Student Center an hour before the event, and the demands in its words—cancel the Bovino event, adopt sanctuary campus protections, and disclose the university's relationship with the speaker. The statement.

SubjectiveColumbia University—“Our Resolution With the Federal Government,” July 23, 2025 (columbia.edu)
The university's own account of its settlement: $200 million over three years to the federal government, $21 million to settle the EEOC investigations, the vast majority of the terminated grants reinstated, an independent monitor, and the agreement's preservation of the university's authority over hiring, admissions, and academic decisions, with no admission of liability. The resolution.

SubjectiveAmerican Association of University Professors—litigation record, AAUP v. Department of Justice and Harvard University v. HHS (aaup.org)
The association's account of the Harvard funding litigation: the September 3, 2025 judgment of Judge Allison D. Burroughs holding the freeze and terminations unconstitutional retaliation, unconstitutional conditions, and coercion in violation of the First Amendment, Title VI, and the Administrative Procedure Act; the government's appeal of December 31, 2025; and argument in the First Circuit on October 5, 2026. The litigation page.

SubjectiveThe Times—investigation of arrests for online communications offences, April 2025 (figures as compiled and fact-checked from the paper's freedom-of-information returns)
The count on which the British section rests: 12,183 arrests in 2023 under section 127 of the Communications Act 2003 and section 1 of the Malicious Communications Act 1988, recorded by the police forces of England and Wales that answered the paper's requests, up from 7,734 in 2019, with fewer than one in ten of those arrested in 2023 sentenced. The offences cover any electronic communication, not social-media posts alone. The fact-check and figures.

SubjectiveUnited Kingdom Government—response to the non-crime hate incidents final report, March 31, 2026 (gov.uk)
The Home Office's announcement accepting the College of Policing and National Police Chiefs' Council review: non-crime hate incidents will no longer be recorded, the statutory code of practice is revoked, a narrower incident standard tied to policing purposes replaces it, and lawful speech is stated not to be a police matter under the new framework. The response.

SubjectiveThe Daily Telegraph—“Inside the Dystopian World of Germany's Free Speech Crackdown,” July 2026 (as syndicated)
The investigation reporting the November 2024 search of the Bavarian pensioner Stefan Niehoff's home over the “Schwachkopf” meme directed at Vice Chancellor Robert Habeck, the complaint that set it in motion, the prosecutors' later decision that the insult lacked sufficient weight, and the police statistics showing investigations into insults against politicians reaching record levels. The report.

SubjectiveVice President J. D. Vance—address to the Munich Security Conference, February 14, 2025 (transcript extracts)
The speech in which the Vice President told the conference that the threat he worried about most was not Russia or China but “the threat from within”: the retreat of Europe from fundamental values shared with the United States, with the Brussels social-media warning and the shutting down of media, elections, and political participation named as the instances. Finland's president and Germany's chancellor rejected the characterization and defended their jurisdictions' regulation of hate speech. The speech, quoted and answered.
