### Jensen Huang: What the Record Shows About the Man Who Ran the AI Age

Filed as: Special Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-14T10:30:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-14-jensen-huang-record.html

Special Report

Santa Clara · The Founder · The Investigation · The Record of 33 Years

Objective

Jensen Huang: What the Record Shows About the Man Who Ran the AI Age

Jensen Huang resigned on November 12, 2026, as president, chief executive, and director of Nvidia, the company he co-founded in a San Jose diner in 1993 and led for 33 years. The board named Colette Kress, the chief financial officer since 2013, interim chief executive and opened a search. The resignation closed a week that began with Huang’s written admission of an extramarital affair and the board’s announcement of an independent investigation into whether he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort—an allegation the board says it has no reason to believe compromised national security or company secrets, and which China has dismissed. This report files the documented record of the man and of the company he leaves: the Kentucky reform school and the Oregon diner dishwasher, the $40,000 founding, the near-bankruptcy of 1996, the gaming company the market priced for two decades, the CUDA bet of 2006, two cryptocurrency stampedes that repriced his chips before artificial intelligence did, and the 2023–2026 ascent that made Nvidia the most valuable company on earth and left its supply chain, its customers’ capital budgets, and two governments’ export law arranged around his product line.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1030 ET, Saturday, November 14, 2026.

On Thursday, November 12, 2026, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as its president, chief executive officer, and a member of its board, effective immediately, ending a tenure that began with the company’s incorporation on April 5, 1993 and ran 33 years without interruption. He was, at the end, the last founder-chief executive standing among the companies that define the era’s technology, and the company he leaves is the one the world’s artificial intelligence is built on: $215.9 billion of revenue in the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026, nine dollars of every ten from data centers; a market value that peaked at about $5.77 trillion on October 6, 2026, the largest ever recorded for a public company; an estimated three-quarters or more of the world’s AI accelerator revenue; a fabrication chain that runs through one foundry and one island; an export-control regime in Washington written, rule by rule, around his part numbers; and some $720 billion of 2026 capital spending by his four largest customers guided substantially toward machines his roadmaps specify. The company gave no reason for the resignation in its announcement. The week that preceded it is documented: on Sunday, November 8, Huang wrote to his employees admitting an extramarital affair and apologizing to his family and his company, and the board announced an independent investigation into whether he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, stating that it had no reason to believe national security or Nvidia’s secrets had been compromised. Reporting by The New York Times had identified the other relationship as Alice Huang, a former executive of the Singapore data-center company Megaspeed, and had reported that United States intelligence agencies concluded she was passing information to Beijing—a conclusion China’s Foreign Ministry has dismissed as an unsubstantiated smear, and on which no charge against any person appears in the record. A second Times report, of an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him, preceded the board’s Wednesday-night meeting; the board accepted his resignation on November 11, and the stock, which had already fallen for five consecutive weeks, lost a further 12.75 percent in the week of his exit and closed Friday below $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025. Behind the week stands the longer file, and the longer file is the subject of this report: a boy sent from Thailand to a Kentucky reform school by clerical mistake, a dishwasher in an Oregon Denny’s, an engineer who founded a company in another Denny’s with $40,000, a chief executive who counted his company’s remaining payroll in weeks in 1996 and in months again in the stock collapses that followed, the maker of a gaming company that the market priced as a gaming company for two decades, and the author of the 2006 bet—CUDA—that sat in his chips for six years before a neural network trained on two gaming cards showed what it was for.

The event, as documented

The sequence opens in print on October 29, 2026, when The New York Times reported that Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based operator of data centers filled with Nvidia chips, and that United States intelligence agencies had determined she was feeding information to Beijing. The two are not related. Megaspeed itself was already a documented object of official attention on two continents: the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security had raised concerns about the company in 2024 over the possible diversion of embargoed chips into China, the matter passed to the FBI in 2025, the Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation according to the Times’s reporting, and Singaporean authorities questioned Alice Huang last year in their own inquiry into Megaspeed and confiscated her passport, finding insufficient evidence of a crime, according to the Boston Globe’s reporting. Megaspeed is reported to have purchased between $2 billion and $4.8 billion of Nvidia chips across the period covered by the published accounts; Nvidia and Megaspeed have each denied any diversion of technology. On Sunday, November 8, the matter moved from the newspapers into the company’s own documents. Huang wrote to Nvidia’s employees, in a letter the company also published: “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” The letter named no other person and tied the admission to “the national security concerns raised in news reports,” adding: “NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.” The board’s accompanying statement expressed confidence in Huang and opened the investigation under its independent directors, assisted by outside legal counsel—CNBC reported the firm as Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz—into whether he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, stating that it had no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia’s confidential information had been compromised. President Trump weighed in the same evening in Huang’s support, calling him, in CNN’s rendering, an “honorable guy.”

The board’s position held for three days. The New York Times then reported a second affair, with an executive who reports directly to Huang; The Wall Street Journal reported on November 11 that directors were preparing to remove him; and CNN’s account of the week records that the board convened Wednesday night, November 11, to weigh the ouster. The filing that closes the sequence is the company’s Form 8-K to the Securities and Exchange Commission: on November 11, 2026, the board accepted the resignation of Jen-Hsun Huang as president, chief executive officer, and board member, effective immediately; appointed Colette M. Kress, 59, executive vice president and chief financial officer since September 2013, to serve as interim chief executive officer while it conducts a search; and appointed Harvey C. Jones, 73, a director and the former chief executive of Synopsys, as the board’s first-ever chair. The announcement issued November 12 states that Kress will hold both offices until a permanent successor is named, that the search will consider internal and external candidates, and that the board expects “the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.” It carries no reason for the resignation and no statement from Huang. It thanks him for his “immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry” and confirms that the company will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on Tuesday, November 17, as previously scheduled.

The allegation at the center of the week stands in the record at a precise and limited strength, and the desk prints it at that strength. What is documented is a set of reports, attributed to United States officials and intelligence agencies in the Times’s and the Financial Times’s reporting, holding that Alice Huang worked with Chinese intelligence and that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. What is also documented is the board’s statement that it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia’s secrets were compromised; China’s Foreign Ministry’s dismissal of the espionage claims as unsubstantiated and a smear; the absence, as of this filing, of any charge against Huang, against Alice Huang, or against Megaspeed in the matter; and the President’s statement, reported by The Hindu BusinessLine, that the FBI is looking into the relationship, with the bureau’s inquiry’s status not established in the public record. The board’s internal investigation continues under its stated scope. Congress has entered the file on its own track: Huang has been summoned to testify behind closed doors on November 18 before three House committees—the Select Committee on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence, according to Le Monde’s account—with a subpoena under discussion if he declines, according to USA Today; and on November 12, Senate Banking Committee Democrats summoned Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify, according to TechCrunch’s timeline of the affair. The market’s own record of the week is arithmetic. Nvidia closed at $178.67 on Monday, November 9, the first session after Huang’s letter; fell to $168.89 Tuesday; recovered to $173.73 Wednesday; and on Thursday, the day of the announcement, fell as much as 14.3 percent intraday before closing at $166.19, down 4.34 percent, for a market value of about $4.01 trillion. On Friday, November 13, it closed at $162.85, down a further 2.01 percent, at about $3.92 trillion—below $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025, CNBC reported. The week’s decline of 12.75 percent removed about $573 billion of market value, the largest weekly loss ever recorded for a company, on Dow Jones Market Data as reported by The Wall Street Journal; it was Nvidia’s sixth consecutive weekly decline, its longest losing streak since 2012, and it extended a fall from the October 6 peak of about $5.77 trillion to roughly $1.85 trillion of erased value. HSBC downgraded the stock to hold on Friday, cutting its target to $170 and citing, in the market reporting of the downgrade, the uncertainty that will prevail until a permanent succession plan is laid out.

The man, from the record

Jen-Hsun Huang was born on February 17, 1963, in Taipei, Taiwan, the younger of two sons of a chemical engineer and a schoolteacher, and spent his early childhood in Tainan and then in Thailand, where his father worked at an oil refinery. In 1973, with unrest rising in Thailand, the boys were sent ahead of their parents to an aunt and uncle in Tacoma, Washington, recent immigrants themselves, who enrolled them at the Oneida Baptist Institute in the mountains of eastern Kentucky in the belief that it was a prestigious boarding school. The Institute was a religious reform academy for troubled youth. Huang was nine or ten years old, too young for its classes, and attended the public Oneida Elementary School while living in the Institute’s boys’ dormitory; he stayed about two years. His parents then reached the United States and settled in Beaverton, Oregon, and the brothers rejoined them. Huang attended Aloha High School in Aloha, Oregon, skipped grades, became a nationally ranked table-tennis player, graduated at sixteen, and worked at a local Denny’s from 1978 into his college years, starting as a dishwasher and working as busboy and waiter. At Oregon State University he studied electrical engineering—chosen, the profiles record, for its low in-state tuition—and graduated in 1984 with highest honors; his engineering lab partner, Lori Mills, became his wife. Recruited by Texas Instruments, AMD, and LSI Logic, he chose AMD and designed microprocessors, then moved to LSI Logic, where he worked on graphics technology for customers including Sun Microsystems and rose to director of the CoreWare division. Across those years he attended Stanford University at night and earned a master’s degree in electrical engineering in 1992, while working full-time and raising two children. The marriage that his November 8 letter addressed had lasted, on TechCrunch’s reckoning, forty years.

A booth on Berryessa Road

At LSI Logic, Huang worked alongside two Sun Microsystems engineers, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, who wanted to build a graphics chip for personal-computer games. Because the planning could not be done at work, the three met in late 1992 at a Denny’s roadside diner on Berryessa Road in East San Jose—neutral territory, in Priem’s later words to The Wall Street Journal. The division of labor agreed there held for the life of the company: Malachowsky took hardware, Priem took software, and Huang took the business. On April 5, 1993, the three incorporated Nvidia with about $40,000 in the bank. Huang, thirty years old, became its president and chief executive, the only chief executive the company would have for the next 33 years. The booth story is the company’s own founding account, retold by all three founders across three decades and commemorated by the company itself: on September 26, 2023, Denny’s chief executive joined Huang at the Berryessa Road restaurant to install a plaque marking the corner booth as the birthplace of what was then a $1 trillion company. The desk distinguishes the strata as the record presents them: the incorporation, its date, the three founders, and the $40,000 stand in reference and company records; the booth, the bullet holes in the diner window that Malachowsky recalls noticing as they left, and the founders’ division of the work are the founders’ own retelling, consistent across every published version, and printed here as their account. The name the three men chose derived from the Latin invidia, envy, with the letters NV standing for their working phrase for the venture, “next version.”

Thirty days from going out of business

The company’s first product nearly ended it inside three years. The NV1, shipped in 1995, rendered three-dimensional graphics with quadrilateral primitives at the moment the industry, following Microsoft’s Direct3D standard, settled on triangles; the chip was incompatible with the direction of the market and failed commercially. Nvidia had compounded the bet by building the graphics chip for Sega’s next console on the same approach. Sega cancelled the console work and switched vendors. What followed is the near-death sequence that Huang himself made the first of the three failure stories in his commencement address at National Taiwan University on May 27, 2023: Sega’s president, Shoichiro Irimajiri, persuaded his board to invest $5 million in Nvidia even with the contract dead, extending the company’s life; Huang laid off more than half of a staff of about one hundred, down to roughly forty; and the surviving team concentrated everything on a single triangle-based chip, the RIVA 128, simulating the design in software because the company could not afford a failed silicon run. When the RIVA 128 shipped in August 1997, Nvidia had about one month of payroll left in the bank. The chip sold about a million units in its first four months and produced the company’s first solid profits. The sentence Huang repeated at company meetings for the rest of his tenure dates from that month, and the desk prints it as the record’s own refrain: “Our company is thirty days from going out of business.” His 2023 telling of the Sega episode to the graduates carries the moral he attached to it: “Confronting our mistake, and with humility asking for help, saved Nvidia.” Nvidia went public in January 1999. The pattern the near-death installed—total concentration on a single architecture, an annual cadence of successors, and a chief executive who treated survival as a monthly condition—is the pattern the next three decades of the record show.

The gaming company

The baseline from which the company’s final ascent is measured is in its own annual reports, and the desk states it plainly because the later figures invite amnesia: for most of its life, in its accounts and in the market’s estimation, Nvidia was a company that made graphics cards for people who play games. In fiscal 2017, the year ended January 29, 2017, the company’s Form 10-K records total revenue of $6.9 billion, of which gaming supplied $4.1 billion, 58.8 percent, and the data center supplied $830 million, 12 percent; about 72 percent of all revenue was associated with the personal-computer platform. Gaming remained the largest single line in the accounts every year through fiscal 2022, when it reached $12.5 billion against the data center’s $10.6 billion. The GeForce line was the company’s public identity, its cash engine, and its channel to the developers who would later matter most; the data-center line, growing at triple-digit rates in the late 2010s on deep-learning demand the fiscal 2017 filing already names, remained a minority interest in a gaming company’s ledger. That is the standing from which the sequence of the next sections proceeds: a bet placed in 2006 inside a gaming company’s product, a decade in which the bet’s returns were real and small next to the gaming line, and two stampedes of buyers who wanted the gaming product for purposes its makers had not designed it for, before the third purpose repriced the entire company.

The bet

In November 2006, alongside the GeForce 8800 graphics chip, Nvidia released CUDA, a software platform that let programmers write general-purpose code for the graphics processor—the same silicon that drew game worlds, exposed as a parallel computer for any mathematics that could be broken into thousands of simultaneous pieces. Huang’s company then spent the better part of a decade paying for the bet out of the gaming business: CUDA’s tooling, libraries, and developer evangelism, and the Tesla data-center line built on it, ran ahead of the revenue they produced, and the company’s filings through the period show the data center contributing a tenth to a fifth of sales while gaming carried the enterprise. The market’s pricing of the period is also in the record: the company that would reach $5 trillion in 2025 carried a market value of roughly $14 billion in 2016, a decade after CUDA’s launch. The inflection the record shows arrived in September 2012, when researchers at the University of Toronto—Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton—entered the ImageNet image-recognition competition with a neural network trained on two of Nvidia’s consumer gaming cards and won by a margin large enough to redirect the field; deep learning, as a practical discipline, moved onto Nvidia’s hardware in that result, because the hardware the result was achieved on was a pair of GeForce cards and the software it ran was CUDA. Huang’s own summary of the episode, from the same 2023 commencement address, compresses the claim to its documented core: “We invented CUDA and pioneered accelerated computing and AI.” The decade’s remaining fact is the financing: gaming revenue grew from $4.1 billion in fiscal 2017 to $12.5 billion in fiscal 2022, and it was that growth, in the company’s own accounts, that funded the data-center build-out through the years when the data center could not yet fund itself.

Repriced twice

Twice before artificial intelligence repriced the company, buyers who were not its intended customers bid up its cards. The first stampede came with the cryptocurrency boom of 2017 and 2018: miners discovered that the parallel processors in gaming cards mined Ethereum efficiently, retail cards grew scarce and sold above list, and Nvidia’s disclosures lagged the phenomenon in a way that later entered the regulatory record. The company disclosed in 2018 that sales of chips to cryptocurrency miners had brought in $289 million in the quarter ended April 2018. In May 2022, the Securities and Exchange Commission settled charges that the company’s fiscal 2018 filings had been inadequate on exactly this point: the Commission found that cryptomining was a significant element of the growth in the company’s gaming revenue across consecutive quarters of that year and that the filings did not disclose it, leaving investors unable to judge how much of the growth would survive the mining market. Nvidia paid a $5.5 million penalty and accepted a cease-and-desist order, without admitting or denying the findings. The second stampede, in 2020 and 2021, was larger. The RTX 30 series launched into the mining boom and into pandemic demand at once; the flagship RTX 3090, listed at $1,499, changed hands above $3,000 in secondary markets, and trade coverage of the period records street prices at two to three times list across the line. The company’s documented response was to split the product in two: mining limiters on the gaming cards, and in February 2021 a dedicated line, the Cryptocurrency Mining Processor, sold under Huang’s stated division—“GeForce is made for gaming. CMP is made for mining”—which recorded $155 million of revenue in its first quarter. The second boom ended by protocol rather than by price: Ethereum’s September 2022 transition away from proof-of-work abolished GPU mining demand for the second-largest cryptocurrency in a single software event, and Nvidia’s revenue for the quarter ended October 2022 fell 17 percent year over year, to $5.93 billion, on the inventory the vanished demand left behind. Eight weeks after that quarter closed, on November 30, 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT. The third stampede—the one that did not end—began there.

The coronation, in numbers

The crossover in the accounts came first. In fiscal 2023, the year ended January 2023, data-center revenue of $15.0 billion passed gaming’s $9.1 billion for the first time, and the generative-AI build-out then compounded the new line at rates the filings record without precedent for a company of Nvidia’s size: data center at $47.5 billion in fiscal 2024, $115.2 billion in fiscal 2025, and $193.7 billion in fiscal 2026, against total company revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65 percent in the final year, with net income of $120.1 billion and two direct customers accounting for 22 percent and 14 percent of all revenue, on the fiscal 2026 Form 10-K. The most recent reported quarter, the second of fiscal 2027, ended July 26, 2026, recorded revenue of $96.2 billion, up 106 percent year over year, with the data center at $89.0 billion. The market-value ladder of those years is a dated record of firsts: $1 trillion on May 30, 2023; $2 trillion on February 23, 2024; $3 trillion on June 5, 2024; $4 trillion on July 9, 2025, a level no public company had reached; $5 trillion on October 29, 2025, also a first; and a peak of about $5.77 trillion on October 6, 2026, at which point the published comparisons placed the company’s value above the gross domestic product of every country except the United States and China. In the index arithmetic that governs household savings, State Street’s SPY holdings file put Nvidia as the S&P 500’s largest constituent at 8.38 percent on September 30, 2026, and at 6.30 percent on November 10, 2026, second to Apple, the weight falling with the share price rather than with any change in the index’s rules. At the March 2026 GTC conference, the company cited roughly $1 trillion of cumulative revenue visibility for its Blackwell and Vera Rubin architectures across 2026 and 2027. Huang stood at the center of the structure in ways the record documents rather than asserts: a shareholding of about 3.6 percent of the company, on USA Today’s reckoning; a public persona built on the black leather jacket he wore at every keynote, including the Computex address in Taipei on June 1, 2026; a management structure in which dozens of executives reported directly to him and no succession plan was in place, on Barron’s account; and his own description of the arrangement to Bloomberg in 2023, preserved in CNN’s report of the resignation: the company “was built so that I know how to run it.” There had never been an Nvidia without Huang; as of November 12, 2026, there is.

What was hanging on the man

The inventory of what the succession now governs can be stated in documented parts, and the desk states it without enlarging it. The product: analyst estimates compiled across 2026 place Nvidia’s share of AI accelerator revenue between roughly 70 and 85 percent, down from a peak near 90 percent as Google’s, Amazon’s, and Microsoft’s in-house silicon grows from a smaller base; Goldman Sachs’s baseline model assigns Nvidia about 75 percent of total compute spending through 2031. Beneath the silicon stands the software: CUDA, twenty years old in 2026, with some 5.9 million developers in the ecosystem industry analyses count, and every major AI framework—PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX—written for it first, which is the mechanism the same analyses name when they call the moat a software moat. The fabrication chain: every flagship Nvidia data-center processor is a TSMC logic die joined to high-bandwidth memory in TSMC’s CoWoS packaging lines in Taiwan; the supplier record compiled by SemiconductorX shows that even the Blackwell wafers TSMC began producing in Phoenix, Arizona, in October 2025 still cross the Pacific to Taiwan for packaging, that industry estimates give Nvidia about 60 percent of TSMC’s CoWoS output in 2026, and that the memory comes from exactly three makers—SK hynix, the largest, Samsung, and Micron—whose 2026 high-bandwidth supply stands fully allocated on their own executives’ statements. The law: the United States export-control regime for advanced computing was constructed, from the October 2022 rules forward, around performance thresholds that capture Nvidia’s product line by name and class—A100 and H100 first, then the China-specific A800 and H800, then the H20, which the government made license-only in April 2025. The fiscal 2026 Form 10-K prices that history: a $4.5 billion charge for H20 inventory and purchase obligations in the first quarter of fiscal 2026, about $60 million of H20 revenue subsequently realized under licenses granted in August 2025, United States officials’ stated expectation, recorded in the filing, of receiving “15% or more of the revenue generated from licensed sales,” and China’s share of company revenue, counted by customer headquarters, falling from 19.2 percent in fiscal 2025 to 9.1 percent in fiscal 2026, with the filing stating that the company had effectively been shut out of China’s data-center compute market. The guidance the interim management now owns repeats the exclusion: the third-quarter fiscal 2027 outlook of about $108 billion of revenue, against analyst expectations of about $109 billion tallied by LSEG, assumes zero data-center compute revenue from China. The demand: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta have guided to a combined $720 billion to $740 billion of capital expenditure for calendar 2026, most of it for AI infrastructure on their own statements, with Goldman Sachs estimating roughly $180 billion of the total flowing to graphics processors and AI accelerators; those four companies’ building programs were specified, in capacity and in timing, against Nvidia’s published roadmaps and allocation decisions, which for three years were Huang’s personal diplomacy as much as his company’s sales process. And the bench that inherits all of it is documented and thin at the top by design: Kress, a finance executive of nearly twenty-five years at Cisco, Microsoft, and Nvidia, who has run Nvidia’s finances since September 2013 and now holds both of its top offices; Jones, the new chair; a layer of operating executives—general counsel Tim Teter, operations chief Debora Shoquist, worldwide field operations head Ajay Puri, hyperscale chief Ian Buck among them—who reported to a chief executive who kept dozens of direct reports and, on the record of the week, no designated successor. The board’s stated expectation, printed above, is continuity without interruption. The first dated test of that expectation arrives Tuesday, November 17, when the company reports its quarter.

The record as it stands on November 14, 2026, is therefore this. A 63-year-old engineer who arrived in the United States as a child, was schooled by mistake in a Kentucky reform academy, washed dishes in an Oregon diner, and founded a company in a California diner with $40,000 in 1993 has resigned, in the ninth week of his company’s sixth consecutive weekly stock decline, every office he held at the company he created. The documented facts of his fall are narrow: an admitted extramarital affair, a second reported affair inside his own reporting line, a board investigation into whether a foreign intelligence service had targeted him through a relationship with an executive of a customer under investigation on two continents, an espionage allegation that the board says it has no reason to believe compromised anything and that the accused country calls a smear, and no charge against any person. The documented facts of his tenure are the wider file: a company carried within a month of payroll in 1996 and rebuilt on a single chip; a gaming company whose own accounts kept gaming as its largest line until 2023; a software bet placed in 2006 that an entire industry’s research enterprise came to stand on; two speculative stampedes that repriced his product before the third one repriced the world’s capital spending; $215.9 billion of revenue in his final full fiscal year, a peak market value of about $5.77 trillion, and a product line around which a superpower wrote its export law and its rival organized its substitution. The investigation continues, the congressional summonses stand for November 18, the earnings arrive November 17, and the search for a permanent successor is open. What the record shows, complete at the hour of filing, is the distance between the two documents the company issued in one week: a founder’s apology on Sunday, and a transition notice on Thursday that thanks him and does not quote him.

The release states no reason for the resignation and carries no statement from Huang. The release.

### Race and Ethnicity: What the Record Shows About the Government's Classification of Americans

Filed as: Special Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-14T10:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-14-race-classification-record.html

Special Report

The Census · Directive 15 · The Naturalization Cases · Virginia · South Africa · France

Objective

Race and Ethnicity: What the Record Shows About the Government's Classification of Americans

The federal government has classified Americans by race since the first census in 1790, and the classifications have never held still. Americans of Middle Eastern and North African origin are White under the standard issued in 1977 and kept in 1997; a revision published March 28, 2024 moves them into a category of their own beginning with the 2030 census; a rule proposed September 10, 2026 would strike the race and ethnicity questions from that census entirely. The courts once decided whiteness applicant by applicant, Virginia's registrar reclassified a people's records by surname, and every regime that held the pencil described its own drawing as progress.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1000 ET, Saturday, November 14, 2026.

The United States government sorts its residents into racial and ethnic categories of its own design, and it revises the design on its own schedule. Under the federal standard issued in 1977 and reaffirmed in 1997, a person having origins in the Middle East or North Africa is White, and has been White in federal statistics for nearly fifty years; more than 3.5 million people reported Middle Eastern or North African descent inside the White category in the 2020 census. A revision of the standard, published in the Federal Register on March 28, 2024, redraws the map: seven minimum categories where the old standard kept five races and a separate ethnicity, one combined question where the old standard asked two, Middle Eastern or North African standing as a category of its own, detailed origins collected by default, full compliance due by 2029, and the 2030 census as the first count under the new design. Implementation has since slipped twice, the Census Bureau has withdrawn its plan to introduce the new questions on its largest survey in 2027, and a rule proposed on September 10, 2026 would bar race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census altogether. The people being classified account for none of these changes. The record behind the current filings runs through two centuries of the same operation: a naturalization statute that admitted “free white persons” and left the courts to decide who they were, applicant by applicant; a federal dictionary of 1911 that counted South Italians as a race apart from North Italians; a Virginia registrar who reclassified his state's Indian families as colored by circular and surname list; a one-drop rule written into a state statute and into census instructions; and, abroad, a South African classification office that had reclassified 18,469 people by 1956 and a French republic whose law forbids the questions entirely. Every version of the system arrived carrying a justification in its era's moral vocabulary. The justifications are part of the record, and this report prints them.

The map in force

The standard that governs most federal data collection today is Statistical Policy Directive No. 15, first issued by the Office of Management and Budget in 1977 and revised once, in 1997. It sets five minimum race categories and treats Hispanic or Latino origin as an ethnicity asked in a separate question. Its definition of the largest category reads, in full: “White. A person having origins in any of the original peoples of Europe, the Middle East, or North Africa.” The Census Bureau's worked examples under that definition list, side by side, entries such as Irish, German, Italian, Lebanese, Near Easterner, Arab, and Polish. The standard states its own nature on its face: the categories, in its words, “are social-political constructs and should not be interpreted as being scientific or anthropological in nature,” and its stated field of use is “Federal statistics, program administrative reporting, and civil rights compliance reporting.” For most of the census's history the answer to the race question was supplied by an enumerator's observation; self-identification spread with the mail-out census around 1970, and the 1977 directive made the respondent the source of the answer as a matter of federal principle. The 1997 revision added one further liberty: beginning with the 2000 census, a respondent could mark more than one race.

The outputs of that map, as measured in 2020, show the instrument at work. The Bureau counted 204.3 million people as White alone and 235.4 million as White alone or in combination. The residual category, Some Other Race, counted 49.9 million alone or in combination and passed the Black or African American population, 46.9 million, as the second-largest group in the country. The population marking two or more races rose from 9 million in 2010 to 33.8 million in 2020, an increase of 276 percent, and the Bureau attributes a large share of the movement to its own redesigned questions and coding procedures, cautioning that comparisons across the decade “should be made with caution” for exactly that reason. The Bureau's linked-record research adds the individual-level figure: matching the same people's answers across the 2000 and 2010 censuses, Liebler and her co-authors found that about 9.8 million people, 6.1 percent of 162 million linked records, gave a different race or Hispanic-origin answer in 2010 than they had given in 2000. The categories held still for that decade. The people inside them moved anyway.

The revision of March 28, 2024

The notice published March 29, 2024, at 89 Federal Register 22182, announced revisions decided the day before, the first since 1997. The revised standard carries seven minimum categories: American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black or African American, Hispanic or Latino, Middle Eastern or North African, Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, and White. Race and ethnicity merge into a single question, with respondents directed to select all that apply. The definition of White contracts to origins in Europe. The new category is defined by origins in the Middle East or North Africa, and the standard requires collection of detail beyond the minimum categories by default: printed example groups and write-in lines under each heading, the examples drawn from the largest groups measured in 2020—Lebanese, Iranian, Egyptian, Syrian, Iraqi, and Israeli under the new heading; English, German, Irish, Italian, Polish, and Scottish under White. The notice states the purpose in its summary: the revisions “are intended to result in more accurate and useful race and ethnicity data across the Federal government.” Agencies were directed to publish implementation plans within eighteen months and to bring every existing collection into compliance by March 28, 2029. The Census Bureau's implementation schedule made the 2030 census the first decennial count under the new map, with the new questions entering the American Community Survey ahead of it.

The case for the new category, as its advocates presented it across more than three decades of campaigning and in the revision's public comment file, is a case about standing in the data: a population counted inside another category cannot be measured for civil-rights enforcement, health disparities, or eligibility for programs allocated by the numbers. Reporting on the announcement recorded the campaign's length—advocates for Arab American and other Middle Eastern and North African communities had sought a category of their own since the standards were young—and the Census Bureau's own research supplied part of their evidence. In the Bureau's American Community Survey records, one in four people of Middle Eastern or North African ancestry did not report White alone, although White was the answer the governing definition assigned them. The 2024 notice's testing record shows what happened when a category was offered: in the Bureau's 2015 National Content Test, respondents of these origins used it in large numbers. The same footnoted record shows the new box fitting some of its assigned peoples loosely. Armenian respondents in panels offered the category chose White 79.0 percent of the time and Middle Eastern or North African 12.6 percent; Sudanese respondents chose Black or African American 87.2 percent and the new category 8.0 percent. The pencil drew a region. The region's peoples, in the government's own test data, distribute themselves across three of its boxes.

The pencil moves again, 2025–2026

The 2024 map stands as the governing standard, and its arrival has been postponed twice. Implementation trackers maintained by the new category's advocates record that the Office of Management and Budget first moved the agency action-plan deadline from September 2025 to March 2026, then to March 2027, and moved the government-wide compliance date from March 28, 2029 to September 28, 2029, seven months before the 2030 census. The Census Bureau's survey schedule moved with it: a December 2025 Federal Register notice proposed adopting the new questions in the 2027 American Community Survey; the supporting documents filed with a May 14, 2026 notice state that the Bureau will not implement the standards in 2027. Then, on September 10, 2026, the Department of Commerce and the Census Bureau proposed a rule, 91 Federal Register 57524, that reaches past delay to removal. Its proposed Part 60 rewrites the residence criteria for the apportionment count. Its proposed Part 70 provides, in the text quoted across the comment file: “no questions about race, ethnicity, or sexual orientation shall appear on the short form of the decennial census questionnaire or any questionnaire used for the enumeration of the population.” The rule's summary defends the removal on the ground that the count should not be, in its phrase, distorted by questions about “immaterial personal characteristics, such as race,” and its preamble asserts that the sole constitutional purpose of the decennial census is the apportionment of the House of Representatives.

The government's own filings argue with the proposal. The Bureau's preliminary regulatory impact analysis, quoted in the comment record by the National Women's Law Center and by a letter from twenty-four United States senators, states that fertility, mortality, cancer, poverty, unemployment, and labor-force rates are produced from decennial counts by race and ethnicity because there are “no other comparably accurate, comprehensive, and reliable sources of this information,” and the senators' letter quotes the filing's own conclusion that the rule “deteriorates the accuracy” of those series. The 2024 notice, two years earlier, had justified the opposite course in the opposite vocabulary: the categories, OMB wrote then, are sociopolitical constructs, and they remain essential to accurate federal statistics and to evaluating how federal programs serve the public. The comment period on the 2026 rule, first set to close October 13, was extended to November 2, 2026 after tribal governments objected to the consultation schedule; the file as it closed carries opposition from the League of Women Voters and the National Network for Arab American Communities, the Native American Rights Fund, the National Academy of Education, and the National Women's Law Center, among others. As of this filing the rule stands proposed. No final rule appears in the record the desk reviewed. The desk therefore prints the state of the question exactly: one federal standard, revised in 2024 and unrepealed, orders a new category drawn for 2030; a second federal document, proposed in 2026 and undecided, would erase the questions the category would be asked in.

Whiteness, the fixed point

Every movement in this record is measured against a single category. The Naturalization Act of 1790 opened citizenship to “any alien, being a free white person,” and Congress extended the statute in 1870 to aliens of African nativity and persons of African descent, leaving every other people on earth to litigate its position relative to one word. Across the following eighty years the federal courts decided the question applicant by applicant, in dozens of reported prerequisite cases, and the two Supreme Court decisions that close the era show the test changing under the pressure of the cases. In Ozawa in November 1922, the Court equated white with “persons of what is popularly known as the Caucasian race” and held a Japanese applicant outside it. Three months later, in United States v. Bhagat Singh Thind, decided February 19, 1923, the applicant's ethnological evidence was conceded and then set aside: a high-caste Hindu of the Punjab, classified by the science of the day as Caucasian and Aryan, was held not white, in an opinion that states the rule in one sentence: “the words ‘free white persons’ are words of common speech, to be interpreted in accordance with the understanding of the common man, synonymous with the word ‘Caucasian’ only as that word is popularly understood.” The case itself was the government's suit to cancel a citizenship already granted. The science had admitted Thind. The common understanding removed him.

The traffic ran the other way for the peoples of the eastern Mediterranean. George Dow, a Syrian immigrant in South Carolina, was denied naturalization by a district judge who read the 1790 statute to cover persons of European nativity or descent and no others. On September 14, 1915, the Fourth Circuit reversed in Dow v. United States, holding on the “generally received opinion” that “the inhabitants of a portion of Asia, including Syria, were to be classed as white persons,” and giving the statute a construction broad enough to include “Syrians, Armenians, and Parsees” within the term. Dow is the direct ancestor of the line in the 1997 standard: the peoples the Fourth Circuit admitted to whiteness by opinion in 1915 are the peoples the Office of Management and Budget carried inside the White definition by directive in 1977, and the peoples the 2024 revision moves out of it. Absorption into the category also proceeded without litigation, by redefinition at scale. The Dictionary of Races or Peoples issued by the federal Immigration Commission in 1911 listed the peoples of Europe as separate races for official purposes and divided Italians at the Apennines: the North Italian “cool, deliberate, patient, practical,” the South Italian “excitable, impulsive, highly imaginative, impracticable,” two distinct ethnic groups in the Commission's ethnology. Federal immigration statistics of the era counted the South Italian as a race in his own right—1,911,933 South Italian admissions recorded between 1899 and 1910, of 2,284,601 Italian admissions in all. Within two generations the two races of 1911 sat inside the single White box of 1977, and the Census Bureau's definition examples print “Italian” with no compass point attached.

The direction of petition reversed across the century, and the reversal is documented at both ends. In 1915 the applicants sued for admission to the White category, because the category carried citizenship; the racial bar to naturalization stood until Congress removed it in 1952. In the decades before 2024, the organized petition ran outward: communities classified White by directive campaigned to be classified separately, because the category now carried invisibility in the data by which civil rights are enforced and disparities are measured. The desk records the constant beneath the reversal. Both petitions were filed with the authority that maintains the category. Both were argued as claims about distance from it—proximity in the courtroom era, when the Syrian's case rested on his closeness to his “neighbors on the European side of the Mediterranean”; separation in the directive era, when the case rested on the distance the existing box concealed. The White category is the axis of the system in both centuries: the largest box on the form, the one every other definition is written against, the one whose boundaries the courts, the commissions, and the budget office have each in turn been asked to police.

The census churn

The decennial form tells the same story in shorter chapters. The first census, in 1790, counted free white males by age, free white females, all other free persons, and slaves. The 1850 census added “mulatto” to the enumerator's marks, and mulatto stayed on the schedule, with interruptions, through 1920. The 1890 census carried the classification to its finest grain: “quadroon,” defined as one-fourth black blood, and “octoroon,” one-eighth or any trace, appeared for that census alone and were dropped in 1900. The 1930 census listed “Mexican” as a race for the first and only time, and its instructions to enumerators carried the one-drop rule in so many words: “a person of mixed white and Negro blood was to be returned as Negro, no matter how small the percentage of Negro blood.” The 1940 census removed Mexican and instructed its enumerators in the opposite direction: “Mexicans are to be regarded as white unless definitely of Indian or other nonwhite race.” A people entered the nation's racial taxonomy in 1930 and exited it in 1940, by instruction sheet. The Pew Research Center's history of the forms, updated November 3, 2025, summarizes the sequence in one line the desk adopts as accurate: the categories have changed from decade to decade, reflecting the politics and science of the times.

One drop, administered

Virginia built the era's most complete state machinery for the same work, and its file survives in detail. State law had long graded legal whiteness by fractions; a person with one-sixteenth or less of black ancestry could stand as white. The Act to Preserve Racial Integrity, passed in March 1924, replaced the fractions with an absolute: a white person was one with “no trace whatsoever of any blood other than Caucasian,” with a single exception—the so-called Pocahontas exception—for persons with one-sixteenth or less of American Indian blood and no other non-Caucasic blood. Birth and marriage certificates were to carry one of two races, white or colored. In 1930 the General Assembly completed the definition from the other side, defining a colored person as anyone with any ascertainable trace of negro blood: the one-drop rule as a statute. The act's administrator was Walter Ashby Plecker, a physician and eugenics advocate who served as registrar of the Bureau of Vital Statistics from 1912 to 1946 and had helped draft the law with the Anglo-Saxon Clubs of America. Plecker held that Virginia contained two races and no third thing; on that doctrine his office reclassified nearly all Virginia Indians as colored on their birth and marriage certificates, circulated lists of surnames, county by county, that it ruled belonged to mixed families, and instructed local registrars, hospital personnel, and school administrators to treat the named families accordingly. Records already issued were altered. The federal census counted 779 Indians in Virginia in 1930 and 198 in 1940. The marriage provisions of the act stood until Loving v. Virginia voided them in 1967; the altered paper stood longer—in 1987, at the request of Virginia Indians, the state vital records office agreed to restore “Indian” on the records of people Plecker's office had reclassified, and no Virginia tribe won federal recognition until 2018.

What the boxes hold

A minimum category is a roll-up, and the contents of the roll-ups are on the record. The 1997 White category spans the original peoples of three landmasses, and the Census Bureau's example entries for it place Irish, German, Italian, Lebanese, Near Easterner, Arab, and Polish in one line. The 2020 census collected more than 350 million detailed responses to its race and ethnicity questions, and its detailed file tabulates 300 detailed race and ethnic groups and 1,187 American Indian and Alaska Native tribes and villages—the plurality inside the boxes, published by the same bureau that administers the boxes. The Black or African American category gathers the descendants of American slavery, the peoples of the African continent, and the Caribbean into one reporting line; the new Middle Eastern or North African category is drawn geographically and takes in, in the Census Bureau's description, Arabic-speaking groups such as Egyptians and Jordanians, non-Arabic-speaking groups such as Iranians and Israelis, and ethnic and transnational groups from the region, such as Assyrians and Kurds—two dozen nations and peoples between Morocco and Iran, filed as one. None of this is concealed. The standards name their purpose in their own text: the categories exist so that statistics can be compared and civil-rights compliance reported against them. The flattening is the price of the comparability, stated in the documents themselves, and the peoples inside each box—their languages, religions, and histories—are the quantity the roll-up sets aside to get it.

Two other answers

The American system is one answer to an administrative question, and the century ran the alternatives at national scale. South Africa's Population Registration Act of 1950 ordered every person in the country classified by the state, and defined its top category by appearance and acceptance: a white person was one who “in appearance obviously is, or who is generally accepted as a white person.” Classification determined residence, schooling, employment, and political rights, and a machinery of officials and Race Classification Boards stood behind the register to correct it. By 1956, on the figures compiled by the South African Institute of Race Relations from the official record, the machinery had reclassified 18,469 people—1,182 reclassified as white, 9,642 as coloured, 7,645 as black—and the Government Gazette was still publishing annual lists of the reclassified in the 1980s, moving individuals among the categories in both directions by administrative act. The act was repealed in 1991. France runs the opposite answer. Its data-protection law of January 6, 1978 prohibits the processing of personal data that reveal, directly or indirectly, racial or ethnic origins, and when Parliament in 2007 voted to permit such processing for studies of diversity and discrimination, the Constitutional Council struck the provision: such processing, the Council held in decision 2007-557 DC, cannot “be based on ethnicity or race” without infringing the Constitution's guarantee of equality without distinction of origin, race, or religion. The consequence stands in France's own words to the United Nations Human Rights Committee in 2009: the Republic is “not in a position to provide statistics disaggregated by ethnic or racial origin.” One state classified everyone and reclassified them by the thousand; one state forbids the ledger; the United States revises its ledger by directive and is currently deciding, in the open, whether to keep it.

Every era's reason

The last entry in the record is the justifications, and they are uniform in one respect: each classifying regime described its system as an improvement, in the vocabulary its era supplied for virtue. The Immigration Commission's dictionary of 1911 presented its racial entries, temperaments included, as science placed at the service of legislation. The Virginia act of 1924 carried its rationale in its title—preservation—and its administrator was a public-health registrar applying eugenics, which the era's universities and medical journals taught as progressive science. The standards of 1977 and 1997 justified uniformity by its uses: comparable statistics and the enforcement of civil-rights law, a rationale printed in the standards themselves. The revision of 2024 justified its new boundaries by accuracy and usefulness, and by the data's role in measuring disparities and evaluating federal programs. The proposed rule of 2026 justifies removal by constitutional fidelity and by the integrity of the count. No document in this file describes its own classification as an exercise of power over the people classified, although classification is the entire content of each document; and no regime in the file describes the regime before it as having acted from the motives it claims for itself. The desk notes the pattern as a property of the documents, not of the men: the self-description is constant across systems whose classifications contradict one another outright, which makes the self-description the one line in each document that carries no information about the system it announces.

The record as it stands on November 14, 2026, is therefore this. The 2024 standards remain the governing federal standard for race and ethnicity data; their implementation has been postponed twice, their introduction on the government's largest survey has been withdrawn, and a proposed rule would bar the questions from the 2030 census, whose comment file closed November 2 with the Bureau's own impact analysis entered against the proposal. The 1997 map still governs the bulk of what the government actually collects, and under it Americans of Middle Eastern and North African origin are White, as they have been since 1977. Behind the current filings stands the longer file this report has printed: a statute of 1790 and the courtrooms that construed it, a dictionary of races, a registrar's surname lists, a one-drop statute, a classification board's annual gazette, a republic that keeps no ledger at all. In every period the classified are the constant and the classifications are the variable, and the hand on the pencil, in every period, belonged to an institution that believed its lines were drawn for the improvement of the society being lined.

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—the desk is filing it, not endorsing it—and each is described in plain terms: what it is and what it says. 14 items.

SubjectiveU.S. Office of Management and Budget—Federal Register notice, 89 FR 22182 (federalregister.gov)
The March 29, 2024 notice announcing the first revision of Statistical Policy Directive No. 15 since 1997: seven minimum categories, a single combined race and ethnicity question, a new Middle Eastern or North African category, detailed collection by default, the working group's research record including the 2015 National Content Test results, and the compliance schedule running to March 28, 2029. The notice.

SubjectiveU.S. Office of Management and Budget—1997 revision of the classification standards (whitehouse.gov)
The October 30, 1997 Federal Register notice carrying the standard still in force for most collections: five race categories, Hispanic or Latino as a separate ethnicity, permission to report more than one race, and the definition of White as origins in the original peoples of Europe, the Middle East, or North Africa. The notice states that the categories are social-political constructs and not scientific or anthropological. The standards.

SubjectiveU.S. Census Bureau—Working Paper No. 108, December 2024 (census.gov)
The Bureau's count of Middle Eastern and North African responses inside the 2020 census race question, where the ancestry had to be written in under White or Some Other Race: over 3.5 million people reported a MENA identity, more than 2.5 million of them MENA alone, with Lebanese, Iranian, and Egyptian the largest detailed groups. The working paper.

SubjectiveU.S. Census Bureau—CES Working Paper 24-14, March 2024 (census.gov)
A Center for Economic Studies paper measuring Middle Eastern and North African identification in American Community Survey data for 2009–2022, reporting that one in four people of MENA ancestry in that period did not select White alone, the answer the governing definition assigns them. The working paper.

SubjectiveU.S. Census Bureau—2020 Census release on the improved race and ethnicity measures, August 12, 2021 (census.gov)
The Bureau's presentation of the 2020 results under the redesigned questions: the Two or More Races population measured at 33.8 million, up from 9 million in 2010, and Some Other Race alone or in combination, at 49.9 million, the second-largest group in the country—with the Bureau's own caution that the improved design and coding account for a large share of the change. The release.

SubjectivePew Research Center—“How U.S. Census Categories Used to Measure Race Have Changed, in 5 Charts,” updated November 3, 2025 (pewresearch.org)
A chart history of the decennial forms from 1790 forward: mulatto added in 1850, quadroon and octoroon confined to 1890, Mexican listed as a race in 1930 only, the 1930 enumerator instructions stating the one-drop rule, and the 1940 instructions directing that Mexicans be regarded as white. The history.

SubjectiveU.S. Supreme Court—United States v. Bhagat Singh Thind, 261 U.S. 204 (1923), opinion text (wikisource.org)
Justice Sutherland's unanimous opinion holding that a high-caste Hindu from the Punjab, conceded to be Caucasian under the ethnology of the day, was not a “free white person” under the naturalization statutes, on the ground that the statutory words are words of common speech, synonymous with Caucasian only as that word is popularly understood. The opinion.

SubjectiveU.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit—Dow v. United States, 226 F. 145 (1915), opinion text (unl.edu; case file, reed.edu)
Judge Woods's opinion reversing the denial of George Dow's naturalization: the court holds that the generally received opinion classed the inhabitants of Syria as white persons, and construes the 1790 statute to include Syrians, Armenians, and Parsees. The Teaching Legal History project at the University of Nebraska republishes the opinion; Reed College's digital exhibit assembles the case file.

SubjectiveJamestown-Yorktown Foundation—“A Heritage Denied: Virginia's Racial Integrity Act” (jyfmuseums.org)
The state museums' account of the 1924 act and of Registrar Walter Plecker's administration of it: the reclassification of Virginia Indians as colored on vital records, the surname lists circulated to clerks, hospitals, and schools, the 1987 agreement to restore “Indian” on request, and the arrival of federal tribal recognition in 2018. The account.

SubjectiveNPR / Central Florida Public Media—report on the revised census boxes, March 28, 2024 (cfpublic.org)
News reporting on the announcement of the 2024 standards: the new Middle Eastern or North African and combined-question design explained, the example groups printed for each category, and the more than three decades of campaigning by Arab American and other MENA advocates that preceded the change. The report.

SubjectiveU.S. Department of Commerce and Census Bureau—proposed rule, 91 FR 57524, and its public comment file (federalregister.gov)
The September 10, 2026 proposal to rewrite the decennial census regulations, including proposed Part 70's bar on questions about race, ethnicity, or sexual orientation, with the comment record as it closed November 2, 2026: the National Women's Law Center comment quoting the Bureau's impact analysis, the Native American Rights Fund comment, the joint League of Women Voters and Arab American communities comment, and a letter from twenty-four senators demanding the rule be rescinded.

SubjectiveYalla Count MENA Coalition—implementation frequently asked questions, July 2026 (yallacountmenain.org)
The advocacy coalition's tracker of the 2024 standards' implementation: the Office of Management and Budget's postponements of the agency action-plan deadline to March 2027 and of the government-wide compliance date to September 28, 2029, recorded as the coalition reported them to the communities the new category covers. The tracker.

SubjectiveSouth African Institute of Race Relations—“Refusing Forced Racialisation at Work,” December 2025 (irr.org.za); South African History Archive heritage project (saha.org.za)
The Institute's occasional paper compiles the official figures for the Population Registration Act's reclassification machinery: 18,469 reclassifications effected by 1956, divided among white, coloured, and black. The History Archive's heritage project documents the Government Gazette's annual publication of reclassification lists, still running in 1984. The paper; the archive.

SubjectiveGovernment of France—follow-up report to the United Nations Human Rights Committee, 2009 (bayefsky.com)
France's own explanation of its statistical practice in reply to the Committee: the 1978 data-protection law's prohibition on data revealing racial or ethnic origins, the Constitutional Council's 2007 decision striking a statutory exception, and the Republic's conclusion that it is not in a position to provide statistics disaggregated by ethnic or racial origin. The report.

### Paris Counts Photography at 200, Tokyo Opens 6,500 Booths, and Thailand Lights Its Rivers

Filed as: Saturday Culture Feature — Weekend Features · 2026-11-14T04:10:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-14-saturday-culture.html

Weekend Features — Saturday Culture

 Objective

 Paris Counts Photography at 200, Tokyo Opens 6,500 Booths, and Thailand Lights Its Rivers

 A curated fair in Paris and an open fair in Tokyo stand at the two ends of the same Saturday: one counts its exhibitors in hundreds and its medium in centuries, the other counts its booths in thousands and admits its artists without a jury. Shanghai closes, Tallinn continues, Jeddah closes, Mexico City opens, two fashion weeks peak on Sunday, Abu Dhabi and Tokyo prepare firsts for next week, and Thailand begins a fortnight of floating lights. The desk files the week in that order.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0410 ET, Saturday, November 14, 2026. The second Saturday Culture Feature of this paper, filed ahead of the day's watches under the Weekend Features ruling of November 4, 2026. International by house rule: no country's framework is applied to another country's culture. The clippings the report was drawn from are filed beneath it, each stamped subjective.

The Week in Brief

The week's cultural centre, measured by what is open this Saturday, is divided between two fairs that could not be built more differently: Paris Photo, in its 29th edition at the Grand Palais, where 242 exhibitors sell and show a medium that turns 200 this year, and Tokyo's Design Festa, in its 64th volume at Tokyo Big Sight, where more than 6,500 booths of original work are open to anyone, professional or amateur, with no jury at the door. Around those two poles the week is full and dated: Shanghai's West Bund Art and Design closes on Sunday, November 15; Tallinn's Black Nights festival is in its middle days, running to November 22 with 489 titles; Jeddah's Wahid exhibition, with more than 60 Saudi and Pakistani artists, closes today; Mexico City's Museo Tamayo opens the Sao Paulo Bienal's travelling exhibition today, to the public on Sunday; two fashion weeks, in The Gambia and in Dubai, hold their main events on Sunday; Abu Dhabi counts five days to the first Frieze fair in the emirate, on November 19; Tokyo counts six days to a new museum's first exhibition, on November 20; and Thailand's Loi Krathong calendar opens on Sunday at Sukhothai, inside a national calendar running November 15 to 29 with the full moon on November 24.

Paris: A Medium Turns 200 Under the Glass Roof

Paris Photo opened on November 12 and runs to Sunday, November 15, and its subject this year is its own age. The fair is in its 29th edition at the Grand Palais, with 242 exhibitors, 195 galleries and 47 publishers from 38 countries, in the fair account filed below. Its programme is built around the Bicentenary of Photography. The Centre Pompidou brings more than 100 works from its collection by nearly 30 artists, arranged in three parts, Making the Image, At Infinity, and Identities. Thomas Ruff is presented in a retrospective hang made with five galleries. The Prix Pictet, founded in 2008, is shown for the first time in the nave. The Main sector holds 150 galleries, and the geography of the stands runs from Bogota and Mexico City to Makati City and Casablanca, in the same account.

The fair's sections divide the medium by its forms, and the oldest forms stand beside the newest. Voices, curated under the title Disappearance, rests on the paradox its curators state in the account: a tool made to preserve what might disappear, celebrated at a time when its traditional form is unstable. Digital, curated by Marco de Mutiis, holds the medium's origins as a technology beside the forms expected to shape seeing next. Emergence carries twenty projects from galleries backing new artists. In the nave, the earliest processes are on the stands themselves: camera clara drawings, photogenic drawings, calotype negatives, daguerreotypes and photograms by the medium's first practitioners, among them Daguerre, Talbot, Girault de Prangey, Anna Atkins and Hippolyte Fizeau, in the same account. A second account filed below gives the fair's scale in rounder numbers, more than 220 exhibitors from over thirty countries, names the Elles x Paris Photo trail for women artists among its sections, and records Ruff's large-scale installation at the entrance. The two counts stand apart in the Cocked Hat.

Tokyo: 6,500 Booths, No Jury, and a Museum That Opens Next Week

Design Festa vol. 64 opens today at Tokyo Big Sight and runs through Sunday, and its rule is admission. The event, born in 1994, is open to anyone with original works, professional or amateur, in the event account filed below. More than 10,000 artists gather at every event. This edition fills the West and South Halls with over 6,500 booths, from 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. both days, with an expected attendance of approximately 140,000 across the two days. Its floor is divided by kind: bright booths and dark booths, live painting completed across the two days in view of the visitors, workshops, a show stage, a food area, and the One Coin Runway, where a visitor takes the stage for 500 yen. A one-day ticket is 800 yen in advance and 1,000 yen on the day. Where Paris selects, Tokyo admits; the two fairs are the week's clearest pair, and the desk prints them as a pair.

Tokyo's second item is an opening that has not happened, announced on November 11 with its dates fixed. MoN Takanawa, the Museum of Narratives in Minato, will present Feel the Sound from November 20, 2026, to March 22, 2027, as part of its opening commemorative programme, produced in collaboration with the Barbican Centre in London, in the museum's announcement filed below. The exhibition is built of installations combining sound, vibration, music and technology, presented as feeling sound with the whole body. This presentation is its first run in Japan, after its original run at the Barbican. A media preview stands on November 19, with tours led by its curator, Luke Kemp. The museum is operated by the East Japan Railway Foundation for Cultural Innovations.

Shanghai Closes, Abu Dhabi Prepares: The Fair Calendar Moves West

West Bund Art and Design closes on Sunday in Shanghai, in the last days of Shanghai Art Week. The fair runs from November 10 to 15 at the West Bund Art Center in Xuhui District. One gallery's account filed below lists its own stand, 1C05, and the artists it carries: Tunji Adeniyi-Jones, Georg Baselitz, Tracey Emin, Mona Hatoum, Damien Hirst, Marguerite Humeau, Yoko Matsumoto, Shigeo Otake, Marina Rheingantz and Tesfaye Urgessa among them, with Antony Gormley, Ibrahim Mahama, Park Seo-Bo, Isamu Noguchi, Liu Wei, Michael Armitage and Etel Adnan also on its list. A single gallery's list is the bearing the desk has for Shanghai this week, and it is printed at that size: it establishes dates, place and one stand's contents, and nothing about the fair's whole.

Abu Dhabi's first Frieze fair opens on November 19, four days after Shanghai closes, and its line-up was published in full on October 22. The inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi runs from November 19 to 22 at Manarat Al Saadiyat, with more than 85 galleries from 67 cities and more than 35 countries and regions, in the fair's account filed below. It joins a network that already runs in London, Los Angeles, New York, Chicago and Seoul. It builds on Abu Dhabi Art's seventeen years in the region, is led by Director Dyala Nusseibeh, and stands among the Louvre Abu Dhabi, the Zayed National Museum and the forthcoming Guggenheim Abu Dhabi. Its main Galleries section holds more than 60 galleries from 56 cities and 32 countries. Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi, selected by Marika Sardar, takes the Indian Ocean as its theme, from antiquity to the early 20th century. Global Futures, selected by Tarini Malik, carries solo presentations. The regional anchoring is named plainly in the account: galleries from the Emirates, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Tehran and Istanbul, beside 20 European galleries.

Tallinn: 489 Titles in the Middle Days

The Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival is the week's longest event still running, and its arithmetic checks. The festival runs 17 days, from November 6 to 22, in its 30th anniversary edition, with 489 titles from 87 countries and regions: 230 features and 259 shorts, which sum to the stated total, in the review file filed below, published on November 13. Its opening film, Ulya, by Latvian director Viesturs Kairiss, is a production of all three Baltic countries, drawn from the life of basketball player Uljana Semjonova. Its two competitions carry 24 films and 21 premieres. The review names the programme's prominent themes as war, displacement, identity, and intergenerational conflict and trauma. The same review prints its own judgment on the festival's standing, largest in scale among the smaller A-list festivals and lowest among them in prestige, and the desk files that judgment as the review's, in the clipping, where a judgment belongs.

Fashion: Two Main Events on One Sunday

Gambia International Fashion Week has been running since November 10, and its main event is Sunday, November 15. The week, in its 4th edition, was founded in 2023 as a non-profit platform for Gambian and African designers, models, creatives and young talent, in the week's account filed below. Its 2026 theme is Roots to Runway, Luxury Born in Gambia, with a stated focus on sustainability, recycling and Made in Gambia. The main event stands at the Sir Dawda Kairaba Jawara International Conference Centre at Bijilo, bringing Gambian and international designers together. Around it, the week carries showcases, cultural experiences, industry conversations and sustainable fashion initiatives to November 17.

Dubai's fashion event is one day long, and it stands on the same Sunday. Dubai Sustainable Fashion Week takes place on November 15 at Atlantis, The Palm, as an initiative of Grupo Zostenible, in the event's own account filed below. Its day is set out in order: morning welcome and networking, midday talks on sustainable fashion and innovation, afternoon designer presentations, evening runway shows, an evening industry panel, and a night media and VIP experience. Its five stated dimensions are runway shows, innovation, global networking, culture and art, and responsible luxury. The same account marks its programme provisional and its full programme as coming soon, with the running order stated in general terms; the desk prints both facts, the date and the provisional programme, at their sizes.

Jeddah Closes Today, Mexico City Opens Today

Wahid closes today in Jeddah, after three days in a consulate. The joint Saudi-Pakistani exhibition opened on November 12 at the Consulate General of Pakistan in Jeddah, with more than 60 artists from both countries, under the theme One Spirit, Shared Heritage, Diverse Expressions, in the exhibition account filed below, published today. Wahid means One. Its programme is visual artworks and traditional Arabic calligraphy; its contributors include Pakistan's Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, Ahmad Farooq, and calligrapher Shafiq-uz-Zaman. Officials of both countries spoke at its opening, and attendance across its three days was by prior registration.

Mexico City's opening today is a travelling exhibition at its last stop. The travelling exhibition of the 36th Bienal de Sao Paulo, Not All Travellers Walk Roads, Of Humanity as Practice, opens at the Museo Tamayo today, November 14, and runs to the public from November 15 to February 7, 2027, with works by 26 artists, curated by Anna Roberta Goetz, in the Bienal's own notice filed below. It is the first time the Bienal's travelling programme has come to Mexico, and the last stop of this edition's tour. The notice stands carried over from last week's file, where the desk filed it ahead of the opening; today the date it named has arrived.

Thailand: A Fortnight of Lights Opens on Sunday

Loi Krathong's national calendar opens on November 15 and runs to November 29, and its centre is a date still ten days off. The festival is observed on the full moon of the twelfth Thai lunar month, which falls on Tuesday, November 24 this year, in the festival account filed below, checked on November 7 against the Tourism Authority of Thailand's calendar and the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration's notices. Decorated baskets are floated as a gesture of gratitude for water; in the north, Yi Peng sky lanterns are released, a separate ritual on the same nights. The fortnight is a map of dated programmes: Sukhothai Historical Park, from November 15 to 24, with candlelight and fireworks in the ancient capital; Bangkok's clusters at Rama VIII Bridge, Phra Sumen Fort, Maha Kan Fort and the Prem Prachakon Canal, with a historical route running from November 17 to 29; Phuket's Saphan Hin, from November 16 to 25; Chiang Saen's Yi Peng on the Mekong, from November 20 to 24; Tak's Loi Krathong Sai, 1,000 floating krathongs, from November 21 to 24; and Chiang Mai's CAD KhomLoi on November 24 and 25. Peak evenings in most cities are November 23 to 25. Saturday therefore stands at the edge of the festival: nothing floats tonight in the national programme, and everything floats within fifteen days.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, Paris Photo's size: 242 exhibitors, 195 galleries and 47 publishers from 38 countries in the fair account, against more than 220 exhibitors from over thirty countries in the second account. The two statements are compatible, since the larger count satisfies the smaller one's floors, and the desk prints the exact count as the fair account's and the floor as the second account's, without merging them. Second, Tokyo's attendance: the 140,000 figure for Design Festa is the event account's expected attendance, published before the doors opened today; it is a published scale, not a counted crowd, and no counted figure can stand in the file until the event has run. Third, Dubai's programme: a full day's running order stands published for November 15, and the same account calls that programme provisional and its full programme still to come; the date is fixed and the contents are general, and both facts stand. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts are single-valued: Paris Photo runs November 12 to 15 in its 29th edition; Design Festa vol. 64 runs November 14 and 15 with over 6,500 booths; West Bund runs November 10 to 15; Tallinn runs November 6 to 22 with 230 features and 259 shorts summing to its stated 489 titles; Wahid ran November 12 to 14 with more than 60 artists; the Bienal's travelling exhibition opens at the Tamayo today and to the public on Sunday; the Gambia and Dubai fashion main events stand on Sunday, November 15; Frieze Abu Dhabi opens on November 19; Feel the Sound opens in Tokyo on November 20; and Loi Krathong's full moon is November 24, inside a national calendar running November 15 to 29. The log proceeds to Saturday's watches.

 The Clippings Filed With This Feature

 Everything the desk read for the feature above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective — a source with a position, printed because it is useful — and described by what it says. The desk's feature is the only item in this file stamped objective. Twelve items.
